markdown:
This example demonstrates the routed MatchBox app server API built around `web.server()` and ColdBox-style handlers:

```boxlang
function( event, rc, prc ) { ... }
```

App-server scripts should import the namespace explicitly:

```boxlang
import boxlang.web;
```

It is a different product from the static/BXM webroot server. Use this app server when you want to build:

* JSON APIs
* lightweight microservices
* middleware pipelines
* signed webhook receivers
* server-rendered endpoints with explicit template rendering
* apps that need explicit static asset mounts inside a routed server

This example is for the native `matchbox_server` binary. ESP32 firmware does not run `web.server()` scripts; it serves files from an `app/` directory instead. See [Building for ESP32](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html). The [Web server guide](/building-and-deploying/web-server/index.html) lists the whole app-server API.

For a websocket-focused example, see [websocket_counter](/examples/websocket_counter/README/index.html).

## Project Structure

* `app.bxs`: Main routed application.
* `public/site.css`: Static asset served through app middleware.
* `views/home.bxm`: Template rendered by `event.setView()`.

## Key Concepts

### 1. The Handler Shape

Each route handler receives three arguments:

* `event`: A native request/response object with ColdBox-style helpers.
* `rc`: The public request collection. Route params, query params, form fields, and top-level JSON object keys are merged here.
* `prc`: The private request collection for passing internal state across middleware and handlers.

### 2. Middleware

Middleware uses a fourth `next` argument:

```boxlang
app.use( function( event, rc, prc, next ) {
    prc.requestStarted = true;
    next.run();
} );
```

Middleware can mutate `rc`, `prc`, `session`, headers, cookies, status codes, and response bodies.

### 3. Templates

Routes can render templates explicitly:

```boxlang
event.setView( "views/home.bxm", {
    "title": "MatchBox"
} );
```

Templates receive:

* `event`
* `rc`
* `prc`
* `session`
* `viewArgs`

### 4. Static Files Middleware

Static assets can be mounted explicitly inside the app server:

```boxlang
app.use( app.middleware.buildStaticFiles( "/assets", "public" ) );
```

This serves files from the `public` directory at `/assets/...`. The directory is resolved relative to the app script root, missing files fall through to the normal app routing path, and traversal outside the mounted directory is blocked.

### 5. Webhook Builder

Webhook endpoints can be declared with a fluent builder. There is no `env` scope; read secrets from the process environment with `getSystemSetting( name, [default] )`:

```boxlang
app.webhook(
    app.buildWebhook()
        .path( "/webhooks/stripe" )
        .secret( getSystemSetting( "STRIPE_SECRET" ) )
        .signatureHeader( "stripe-signature" )
        .prefix( "sha256=" )
        .timestampHeader( "stripe-timestamp" )
        .toleranceSeconds( 300 )
        .replayHeader( "stripe-event-id" )
        .replayTtlSeconds( 300 ),
    function( event, rc, prc ) {
        event.renderText( "ok" );
    }
);
```

## Running the Example

The `--app` flag belongs to the `matchbox_server` binary, which you build from the MatchBox source tree. `matchbox app.bxs` cannot run this script. From the project root:

```bash
cargo run -p matchbox_server -- --app docs/examples/app_server/app.bxs
```

The address comes from `app.listen( 8090 )` in the script, which binds `127.0.0.1`. To listen on all interfaces pass a struct: `app.listen( { "host": "0.0.0.0", "port": 8090 } )`.

Then visit:

* `http://localhost:8090/`
* `http://localhost:8090/api/hello/MatchBox`
* `http://localhost:8090/assets/site.css`

The script is compiled once, but its top level runs again on every request. Reload `/` to see the visit count in `session.visitCount` rise: session data is kept by the `MBX_SESSION_ID` cookie, while a plain variable at the top of the script would reset on each request.

## What The Example Covers

* app-level middleware
* route groups
* cookies
* in-memory session state
* JSON responses
* static asset serving with `app.middleware.buildStaticFiles()`
* template rendering with `setView()`
* signed webhook route registration
* for websockets, see the dedicated websocket counter example

title: Arrays and structs
body: An array is an ordered list. A struct is a set of named values, like an object or a dictionary. Between them they cover most of the data you will handle. Arrays Array positions start at 1 , not 0. This surprises people coming from JavaScript or Rust, so it is worth a run. colors = [ "red", "green", "blue" ]; println( colors[ 1 ] ); println( colors.len() ); colors.append( "violet" ); println( colors.toList( ", " ) ); colors[ 2 ] = "lime"; println( colors.toList( ", " ) ); println( colors[ 1 ] & " to " & colors[ colors.len() ] ); Output: red 3 red, green, blue, violet red, lime, blue, violet red to violet toList turns an array into a delimited string, which is handy for printing. append , prepend , pop and shift add and remove items. Sorting changes the array in place: scores = [ 30, 4, 100, 12 ]; arraySort( scores, "numeric" ); println( scores.toList( "," ) ); Output: 4,12,30,100 Structs person = { name: "Ada", city: "London" }; println( person.name ); println( person[ "city" ] ); person.age = 36; println( structCount( person ) ); println( person.keyExists( "age" ) ); println( person.keyExists( "email" ) ); structDelete( person, "city" ); println( structCount( person ) ); Output: Ada London 3 true false 2 Reach a value with a dot or with brackets. Brackets let you use a key that is stored in a variable. Assigning to a new key adds it. Nesting Arrays and structs nest freely, which is how most real data looks. person = { name: "Ada", langs: [ "BoxLang", "Rust" ] }; println( person.langs[ 2 ] ); people = [ { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "Linus", age: 28 } ]; for ( p in people ) { println( p.name & " is " & p.age ); } Output: Rust Ada is 36 Linus is 28 Loops for ( n in [ 10, 20, 30 ] ) { println( n ); } for ( i = 1; i <= 3; i++ ) { println( "round " & i ); } total = 0; for ( n in 1..4 ) { total += n; } println( total ); count = 0; while ( count < 3 ) { count += 1; } println( count ); for ( key, value in { a: 1, b: 2 } ) { println( key & "=" & value ); } Output: 10 20 30 round 1 round 2 round 3 10 3 a=1 b=2 1..4 is a range. for ( key, value in struct ) walks a struct. Do not rely on the order of struct keys. Try it Add a println inside the people loop that only prints people older than 30. You will need an if , which lesson 7 covers in depth, but you can guess the shape.

title: Async and futures
body: A future represents a result that may not be ready yet. runAsync() starts work and returns a future; get() waits for its result. Starting work slow = runAsync( () => { sleep( 30 ); return "slow"; } ); fast = runAsync( () => "fast" ); println( fast.get() & " then " & slow.get() ); println( runAsync( () => 4 ).then( value => value * 2 ).get() ); fast then slow 8 Use then() to transform a result when it arrives. asyncAllApply( items, callback ) applies a function to a collection and returns the results. Handling errors Errors from asynchronous work surface when you collect the result. Use try / catch , or provide a recovery callback: result = runAsync( () => { throw( message = "unavailable" ); } ).exceptionally( error => "fallback" ); println( result.get() ); fallback See error handling for normal catch and cleanup patterns. Concurrency BoxLang futures take turns on the VM's thread. Native I/O can run independently, but CPU-heavy BoxLang callbacks do not spread across multiple cores. sleep() yields to other tasks rather than making computation parallel. The browser playground uses the same cooperative model and stops runs after five seconds. For a guided introduction, see the async lesson .

title: AWS Lambda
body: MatchBox runs on Lambda's provided.al2023 custom runtime. The package is a bootstrap executable plus your .bx files. On each invocation the runtime loads a BoxLang class and calls its run method with the event. See the single-file Lambda example for a complete project. Handler contract class { function run( event, context, response ) { response.statusCode = 200; response.body = { "message": "Hello" }; } } Argument Contents event The invocation event JSON converted to BoxLang structs, arrays and simple values. context The Lambda context object, below. response A struct with statusCode (200), headers , cookies (empty array), body (empty string) and isBase64Encoded . Change it in place, or return a value. The runtime builds the HTTP-style result from the response: If run returns a struct that has any of statusCode , headers , cookies , body or isBase64Encoded , that struct is the response. If run returns any other value except null , it replaces response.body . A string body is sent as is. Binary data is Base64-encoded and isBase64Encoded is set to true . Any other value is serialized as JSON. headers starts as Content-Type: application/json and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * . If you assign a new headers struct, those defaults are not added , so the CORS header is gone too. An empty headers struct at the end gets the two defaults back. Context Method Returns getAwsRequestId() The request id from the Runtime API. local-request in a local invoke. getFunctionName() , getFunctionVersion() , getInvokedFunctionArn() From AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME , AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION and the invocation headers. getMemoryLimitInMB() From AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE . getLogGroupName() , getLogStreamName() From AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME and AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME . getRemainingTimeInMillis() Time to the invocation deadline. A local invoke always reports 30000. getLogger().log( message, [level="INFO"] ) Writes [LEVEL] message to standard output. getClientContext() , getIdentity() An empty struct. Routing to classes The class that runs is chosen from the request path: The path comes from requestContext.http.path , else rawPath (when requestContext.domainName exists), else requestContext.resourcePath , else path . The first path segment is converted to PascalCase, splitting on characters that are not letters or digits: /hello-world/x becomes HelloWorld.bx . If that file exists in the package root or in src/main/bx/ , it handles the request. Otherwise, and for / or an event with no path, Lambda.bx handles it. Lambda.bx is looked up in the package root, then in src/main/bx/ . Without it the runtime stops at startup with Lambda.bx not found . Application.bx lifecycle An Application.bx in the package root or in src/main/bx/ is optional. On every invocation the runtime creates a new VM, runs Application.bx , constructs it and calls its hooks. Nothing is cached between invocations, so onApplicationStart runs every time and the startup cost is paid per request. Hook When Arguments onApplicationStart() Before the handler class is loaded. none onRequestStart( path, event, context ) Before run . path is the file path of the handler class. onRequestEnd( path, event, context ) After run , also after a failure. onError( error, "", event, context ) When run throws. error is the error text. Hooks you do not define are skipped. After a failure the runtime posts { "errorMessage": ..., "errorType": "MatchBoxLambdaError" } to the Runtime API error endpoint. Local invoke matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json matchbox lambda invoke ./my-project --event event.json The argument is a .bx file or a project directory. The command runs the same code as Lambda, prints the response as JSON, and uses the local defaults above for the context. Deploy matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \ --function matchbox-hello \ --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 \ --public \ --bootstrap /path/to/bootstrap Put the path to the file or project right after deploy , before any flag. The command takes the first argument that does not start with -- as the path. Flag Meaning --function <name> Required. Function name. --bootstrap <file> Required. A Linux executable for the chosen architecture. It is stored in the zip as bootstrap . --role <arn> Execution role. Required when the function does not exist yet. --arch arm64\|x86_64 Architecture for a new function and for the bootstrap you supply. Default arm64 . --out <file> Where to write the zip. Default target/lambda/<function>.zip . --memory <MB> Memory size, applied with update-function-configuration . --timeout <seconds> Timeout, applied with update-function-configuration . --profile <name> , --region <region> Passed to every aws call. --public Create or update a Function URL with auth type NONE . Anyone can call it. Adds the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions for principal * . --url Create or update a Function URL with AWS_IAM auth. Callers must sign requests. Use at most one of --public and --url . Without either, no Function URL is touched. The URL is printed when one is configured. The command writes the zip, checks for the function with lambda get-function , then either runs update-function-code or, when it does not exist, create-function with --runtime provided.al2023 --handler bootstrap . --memory and --timeout are applied afterwards when given. Memory and timeout are numbers up to 65535. Supply the Lambda runtime executable with --bootstrap ; the deploy command does not build it for you. Package layout The zip stores files without compression. bootstrap has mode 0755. Input Contents of the zip A single .bx file The file as Lambda.bx , every other .bx file in the same directory (not subdirectories), boxlang.json and boxlang_modules/ from that directory. A project directory with src/main/bx/ The whole src/main/bx/ tree at the zip root, src/resources/boxlang.json or boxlang.json , and src/resources/boxlang_modules/ or boxlang_modules/ . A project directory without it The .bx files in the directory root plus the same boxlang.json and boxlang_modules/ rules. Only files ending in .bx are picked up outside boxlang_modules/ . Building the bootstrap The bootstrap binary is the matchbox_lambda_runner crate. The release workflow does not publish it. Build it from the MatchBox source tree: cargo build --release -p matchbox_lambda_runner # result: target/release/matchbox_lambda_runner For a different architecture add --target with the matching Rust target, such as aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu for arm64 , and the linker that target needs. Pass the resulting file to --bootstrap . At start the binary reads these variables: Variable Use AWS_LAMBDA_RUNTIME_API Required. Host and port of the Runtime API. LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT Directory with the package. Default /var/task . AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME , AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION , AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE , AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME , AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME Filled into the context. It then loops: fetch the next invocation, run it, post the response or the error. AWS account setup These steps prepare an AWS account and machine for matchbox lambda deploy . 1. Install AWS CLI v2 matchbox lambda deploy shells out to the aws CLI, so install AWS CLI version 2 and verify it is on your PATH . On macOS, the official installer is: curl -o /tmp/AWSCLIV2.pkg https://awscli.amazonaws.com/AWSCLIV2.pkg sudo installer -pkg /tmp/AWSCLIV2.pkg -target / aws --version Expected shape: aws-cli/2.x.x ... AWS CLI v1 and v2 both use the aws command name. If aws --version shows v1, upgrade or fix your PATH before testing deploys. 2. Configure Credentials Recommended: use IAM Identity Center / SSO if your AWS account supports it. aws configure sso --profile matchbox-dev aws sso login --profile matchbox-dev The wizard asks for: SSO start URL SSO region AWS account permission set / role default region output format Use json for output format. If you are using access keys instead of SSO: aws configure --profile matchbox-dev This writes config under: ~/.aws/config ~/.aws/credentials Do not use root account credentials. 3. Pick a Lambda region Choose a region that supports Lambda Function URLs. For example: export AWS_PROFILE=matchbox-dev export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 Or pass them to the deploy command: matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 \ ... 4. Verify your identity Run: aws sts get-caller-identity \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 You should see JSON with: { "UserId": "...", "Account": "123456789012", "Arn": "..." } Keep the Account value handy. 5. Create a Lambda execution role Creating a function requires an existing Lambda execution role ARN. The deploy command does not create IAM roles. Create a trust policy: cat > /tmp/matchbox-lambda-trust-policy.json <<'JSON' { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] } JSON Create the role: aws iam create-role \ --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \ --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/matchbox-lambda-trust-policy.json \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Attach the basic CloudWatch Logs policy: aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Get the role ARN: aws iam get-role \ --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \ --query 'Role.Arn' \ --output text \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Save that ARN. It will look like: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution IAM role propagation can take a few seconds. If Lambda create fails with a role-assumption error immediately after creating the role, wait briefly and retry. 6. Permissions your AWS principal needs The AWS profile you use for deploys needs permissions roughly equivalent to: lambda:GetFunction lambda:CreateFunction lambda:UpdateFunctionCode lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig lambda:GetFunctionUrlConfig lambda:AddPermission iam:PassRole for the execution role ARN If you create the role yourself with the commands above, your principal also needs: iam:CreateRole iam:AttachRolePolicy iam:GetRole Manual AWS CLI equivalents matchbox lambda deploy runs AWS CLI calls like these: aws lambda create-function \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --runtime provided.al2023 \ --handler bootstrap \ --architectures arm64 \ --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \ --zip-file fileb://target/lambda/matchbox-hello.zip \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 aws lambda update-function-code \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --zip-file fileb://target/lambda/matchbox-hello.zip \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 aws lambda create-function-url-config \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --auth-type NONE \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 aws lambda add-permission \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --statement-id FunctionURLAllowPublicAccess \ --action lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl \ --principal "*" \ --function-url-auth-type NONE \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 aws lambda get-function-url-config \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --query FunctionUrl \ --output text \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Sources AWS CLI v2 install guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html AWS CLI SSO configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html AWS CLI prerequisites and credential guidance: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-prereqs.html Lambda Function URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/urls-configuration.html AWS CLI create-function-url-config : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/lambda/create-function-url-config.html AWS CLI add-permission : https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/lambda/add-permission.html
markdown:
MatchBox runs on Lambda's `provided.al2023` custom runtime. The package is a `bootstrap` executable plus your `.bx` files. On each invocation the runtime loads a BoxLang class and calls its `run` method with the event.

See the [single-file Lambda example](/examples/aws_lambda_single_file/README/index.html) for a complete project.

## Handler contract

    class {
        function run( event, context, response ) {
            response.statusCode = 200;
            response.body = { "message": "Hello" };
        }
    }

| Argument   | Contents                                                                                                                                                  |
|:-----------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `event`    | The invocation event JSON converted to BoxLang structs, arrays and simple values.                                                                         |
| `context`  | The Lambda context object, below.                                                                                                                         |
| `response` | A struct with `statusCode` (200), `headers`, `cookies` (empty array), `body` (empty string) and `isBase64Encoded`. Change it in place, or return a value. |

The runtime builds the HTTP-style result from the response:

* If `run` returns a struct that has any of `statusCode`, `headers`, `cookies`, `body` or `isBase64Encoded`, that struct is the response.
* If `run` returns any other value except `null`, it replaces `response.body`.
* A string body is sent as is. Binary data is Base64-encoded and `isBase64Encoded` is set to `true`. Any other value is serialized as JSON.
* `headers` starts as `Content-Type: application/json` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. If you assign a new `headers` struct, **those defaults are not added** , so the CORS header is gone too. An empty `headers` struct at the end gets the two defaults back.

### Context

| Method                                                                 | Returns                                                                                    |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `getAwsRequestId()`                                                    | The request id from the Runtime API. `local-request` in a local invoke.                    |
| `getFunctionName()`, `getFunctionVersion()`, `getInvokedFunctionArn()` | From `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME`, `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION` and the invocation headers. |
| `getMemoryLimitInMB()`                                                 | From `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE`.                                                    |
| `getLogGroupName()`, `getLogStreamName()`                              | From `AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME` and `AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME`.                         |
| `getRemainingTimeInMillis()`                                           | Time to the invocation deadline. A local invoke always reports 30000.                      |
| `getLogger().log( message, [level="INFO"] )`                           | Writes `[LEVEL] message` to standard output.                                               |
| `getClientContext()`, `getIdentity()`                                  | An empty struct.                                                                           |

## Routing to classes

The class that runs is chosen from the request path:

1. The path comes from `requestContext.http.path`, else `rawPath` (when `requestContext.domainName` exists), else `requestContext.resourcePath`, else `path`.
2. The first path segment is converted to PascalCase, splitting on characters that are not letters or digits: `/hello-world/x` becomes `HelloWorld.bx`.
3. If that file exists in the package root or in `src/main/bx/`, it handles the request. Otherwise, and for `/` or an event with no path, `Lambda.bx` handles it.

`Lambda.bx` is looked up in the package root, then in `src/main/bx/`. Without it the runtime stops at startup with `Lambda.bx not found`.

## Application.bx lifecycle

An `Application.bx` in the package root or in `src/main/bx/` is optional. On **every invocation** the runtime creates a new VM, runs `Application.bx`, constructs it and calls its hooks. Nothing is cached between invocations, so `onApplicationStart` runs every time and the startup cost is paid per request.

| Hook                                     | When                                                        | Arguments |
|:-----------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:----------|
| `onApplicationStart()`                   | Before the handler class is loaded.                         | none      |
| `onRequestStart( path, event, context )` | Before `run`. `path` is the file path of the handler class. |           |
| `onRequestEnd( path, event, context )`   | After `run`, also after a failure.                          |           |
| `onError( error, "", event, context )`   | When `run` throws. `error` is the error text.               |           |

Hooks you do not define are skipped. After a failure the runtime posts `{ "errorMessage": ..., "errorType": "MatchBoxLambdaError" }` to the Runtime API error endpoint.

## Local invoke

```sh
matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json
matchbox lambda invoke ./my-project --event event.json
```

The argument is a `.bx` file or a project directory. The command runs the same code as Lambda, prints the response as JSON, and uses the local defaults above for the context.

## Deploy

```sh
matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \
  --function matchbox-hello \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --public \
  --bootstrap /path/to/bootstrap
```

Put the path to the file or project right after `deploy`, before any flag. The command takes the first argument that does not start with `--` as the path.

| Flag                                    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                   |
|:----------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--function <name>`                     | Required. Function name.                                                                                                                                                  |
| `--bootstrap <file>`                    | Required. A Linux executable for the chosen architecture. It is stored in the zip as `bootstrap`.                                                                         |
| `--role <arn>`                          | Execution role. Required when the function does not exist yet.                                                                                                            |
| `--arch arm64\|x86_64`                  | Architecture for a new function and for the bootstrap you supply. Default `arm64`.                                                                                        |
| `--out <file>`                          | Where to write the zip. Default `target/lambda/<function>.zip`.                                                                                                           |
| `--memory <MB>`                         | Memory size, applied with `update-function-configuration`.                                                                                                                |
| `--timeout <seconds>`                   | Timeout, applied with `update-function-configuration`.                                                                                                                    |
| `--profile <name>`, `--region <region>` | Passed to every `aws` call.                                                                                                                                               |
| `--public`                              | Create or update a Function URL with auth type `NONE`. Anyone can call it. Adds the `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` and `lambda:InvokeFunction` permissions for principal `*`. |
| `--url`                                 | Create or update a Function URL with `AWS_IAM` auth. Callers must sign requests.                                                                                          |

Use at most one of `--public` and `--url`. Without either, no Function URL is touched. The URL is printed when one is configured.

The command writes the zip, checks for the function with `lambda get-function`, then either runs `update-function-code` or, when it does not exist, `create-function` with `--runtime provided.al2023 --handler bootstrap`. `--memory` and `--timeout` are applied afterwards when given. Memory and timeout are numbers up to 65535.

Supply the Lambda runtime executable with `--bootstrap`; the deploy command does not build it for you.

### Package layout

The zip stores files without compression. `bootstrap` has mode 0755.

| Input                                   | Contents of the zip                                                                                                                                        |
|:----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A single `.bx` file                     | The file as `Lambda.bx`, every other `.bx` file in the same directory (not subdirectories), `boxlang.json` and `boxlang_modules/` from that directory.     |
| A project directory with `src/main/bx/` | The whole `src/main/bx/` tree at the zip root, `src/resources/boxlang.json` or `boxlang.json`, and `src/resources/boxlang_modules/` or `boxlang_modules/`. |
| A project directory without it          | The `.bx` files in the directory root plus the same `boxlang.json` and `boxlang_modules/` rules.                                                           |

Only files ending in `.bx` are picked up outside `boxlang_modules/`.

### Building the bootstrap

The `bootstrap` binary is the `matchbox_lambda_runner` crate. The release workflow does not publish it. Build it from the MatchBox source tree:

```sh
cargo build --release -p matchbox_lambda_runner
# result: target/release/matchbox_lambda_runner
```

For a different architecture add `--target` with the matching Rust target, such as `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` for `arm64`, and the linker that target needs. Pass the resulting file to `--bootstrap`.

At start the binary reads these variables:

| Variable                                                                                                                                                | Use                                              |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| `AWS_LAMBDA_RUNTIME_API`                                                                                                                                | Required. Host and port of the Runtime API.      |
| `LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT`                                                                                                                                      | Directory with the package. Default `/var/task`. |
| `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME`, `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION`, `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE`, `AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME`, `AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME` | Filled into the context.                         |

It then loops: fetch the next invocation, run it, post the response or the error.

## AWS account setup

These steps prepare an AWS account and machine for `matchbox lambda deploy`.

### 1. Install AWS CLI v2

`matchbox lambda deploy` shells out to the `aws` CLI, so install AWS CLI version 2 and verify it is on your `PATH`.

On macOS, the official installer is:

```bash
curl -o /tmp/AWSCLIV2.pkg https://awscli.amazonaws.com/AWSCLIV2.pkg
sudo installer -pkg /tmp/AWSCLIV2.pkg -target /
aws --version
```

Expected shape:

```text
aws-cli/2.x.x ...
```

AWS CLI v1 and v2 both use the `aws` command name. If `aws --version` shows v1, upgrade or fix your `PATH` before testing deploys.

### 2. Configure Credentials

Recommended: use IAM Identity Center / SSO if your AWS account supports it.

```bash
aws configure sso --profile matchbox-dev
aws sso login --profile matchbox-dev
```

The wizard asks for:

* SSO start URL
* SSO region
* AWS account
* permission set / role
* default region
* output format

Use `json` for output format.

If you are using access keys instead of SSO:

```bash
aws configure --profile matchbox-dev
```

This writes config under:

```text
~/.aws/config
~/.aws/credentials
```

Do not use root account credentials.

### 3. Pick a Lambda region

Choose a region that supports Lambda Function URLs. For example:

```bash
export AWS_PROFILE=matchbox-dev
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
```

Or pass them to the deploy command:

```bash
matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1 \
  ...
```

### 4. Verify your identity

Run:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

You should see JSON with:

```json
{
  "UserId": "...",
  "Account": "123456789012",
  "Arn": "..."
}
```

Keep the `Account` value handy.

### 5. Create a Lambda execution role

Creating a function requires an existing Lambda execution role ARN. The deploy command does not create IAM roles.

Create a trust policy:

```bash
cat > /tmp/matchbox-lambda-trust-policy.json <<'JSON'
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
JSON
```

Create the role:

```bash
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \
  --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/matchbox-lambda-trust-policy.json \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

Attach the basic CloudWatch Logs policy:

```bash
aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

Get the role ARN:

```bash
aws iam get-role \
  --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \
  --query 'Role.Arn' \
  --output text \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

Save that ARN. It will look like:

```text
arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution
```

IAM role propagation can take a few seconds. If Lambda create fails with a role-assumption error immediately after creating the role, wait briefly and retry.

### 6. Permissions your AWS principal needs

The AWS profile you use for deploys needs permissions roughly equivalent to:

* `lambda:GetFunction`
* `lambda:CreateFunction`
* `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode`
* `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration`
* `lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig`
* `lambda:GetFunctionUrlConfig`
* `lambda:AddPermission`
* `iam:PassRole` for the execution role ARN

If you create the role yourself with the commands above, your principal also needs:

* `iam:CreateRole`
* `iam:AttachRolePolicy`
* `iam:GetRole`

### Manual AWS CLI equivalents

`matchbox lambda deploy` runs AWS CLI calls like these:

```bash
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name matchbox-hello \
  --runtime provided.al2023 \
  --handler bootstrap \
  --architectures arm64 \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \
  --zip-file fileb://target/lambda/matchbox-hello.zip \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

```bash
aws lambda update-function-code \
  --function-name matchbox-hello \
  --zip-file fileb://target/lambda/matchbox-hello.zip \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

```bash
aws lambda create-function-url-config \
  --function-name matchbox-hello \
  --auth-type NONE \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

```bash
aws lambda add-permission \
  --function-name matchbox-hello \
  --statement-id FunctionURLAllowPublicAccess \
  --action lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl \
  --principal "*" \
  --function-url-auth-type NONE \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

```bash
aws lambda get-function-url-config \
  --function-name matchbox-hello \
  --query FunctionUrl \
  --output text \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1
```

## Sources

* AWS CLI v2 install guide: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html>
* AWS CLI SSO configuration: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html>
* AWS CLI prerequisites and credential guidance: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-prereqs.html>
* Lambda Function URLs: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/urls-configuration.html>
* AWS CLI `create-function-url-config`: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/lambda/create-function-url-config.html>
* AWS CLI `add-permission`: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/lambda/add-permission.html>

title: Basic BoxLang project
body: This example shows a minimal multi-file BoxLang project with a script entry point and model classes split across separate files - the most common project structure for a BoxLang application. Project Layout basic_project/ ├── main.bxs ← entry point (run this) └── models/ ├── ISpeakable.bxs ← interface definition ├── Animal.bxs ← base class └── Dog.bxs ← class that implements ISpeakable Running Run the project directly with the MatchBox interpreter from this directory: matchbox main.bxs Expected output: === MatchBox Basic Project === --- Descriptions --- I am Whiskers and I make the sound 'Meow' I am Rex and I make the sound 'Woof' --- Speak --- Meow! Rex barks: Woof! Woof! --- Dog Only --- Rex fetches the ball! Rex fetches the frisbee! --- Roster --- Whiskers - Cat Rex - Dog All done! Compile to Bytecode Compile to a portable .bxb bytecode file for faster repeated execution: matchbox --build main.bxs matchbox main.bxb Compile to a Native Binary Produce a single self-contained executable with no runtime to install. The file combines the MatchBox runner and your bytecode: matchbox --target native main.bxs ./main Key Concepts Concept Where to look Class definition models/Animal.bxs Interface models/ISpeakable.bxs , implemented with implements="ISpeakable" in models/Dog.bxs Multi-file imports main.bxs ( import models.Animal ) Struct literals main.bxs (roster array) For-in loop main.bxs (roster iteration) How Multi-File Imports Work MatchBox resolves imports using dot-separated paths relative to the directory where matchbox is invoked. import models.Animal maps to models/Animal.bxs relative to the current working directory. Always run matchbox main.bxs from the basic_project/ directory so that the models.* imports resolve correctly.
markdown:
This example shows a minimal multi-file BoxLang project with a script entry point
and model classes split across separate files - the most common project structure
for a BoxLang application.

## Project Layout

    basic_project/
    ├── main.bxs            ← entry point (run this)
    └── models/
        ├── ISpeakable.bxs  ← interface definition
        ├── Animal.bxs      ← base class
        └── Dog.bxs         ← class that implements ISpeakable

## Running

Run the project directly with the MatchBox interpreter from this directory:

```bash
matchbox main.bxs
```

Expected output:

    === MatchBox Basic Project ===

    --- Descriptions ---
    I am Whiskers and I make the sound 'Meow'
    I am Rex and I make the sound 'Woof'

    --- Speak ---
    Meow!
    Rex barks: Woof! Woof!

    --- Dog Only ---
    Rex fetches the ball!
    Rex fetches the frisbee!

    --- Roster ---
      Whiskers - Cat
      Rex - Dog

    All done!

## Compile to Bytecode

Compile to a portable `.bxb` bytecode file for faster repeated execution:

```bash
matchbox --build main.bxs
matchbox main.bxb
```

## Compile to a Native Binary

Produce a single self-contained executable with no runtime to install. The file combines the MatchBox runner and your bytecode:

```bash
matchbox --target native main.bxs
./main
```

## Key Concepts

|      Concept       |                                      Where to look                                      |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Class definition   | `models/Animal.bxs`                                                                     |
| Interface          | `models/ISpeakable.bxs`, implemented with `implements="ISpeakable"` in `models/Dog.bxs` |
| Multi-file imports | `main.bxs` (`import models.Animal`)                                                     |
| Struct literals    | `main.bxs` (roster array)                                                               |
| For-in loop        | `main.bxs` (roster iteration)                                                           |

## How Multi-File Imports Work

MatchBox resolves imports using dot-separated paths relative to the directory
where `matchbox` is invoked. `import models.Animal` maps to `models/Animal.bxs`
relative to the current working directory.

Always run `matchbox main.bxs` from the `basic_project/` directory so that the
`models.*` imports resolve correctly.

title: BoxLang and Alpine.js
body: This example demonstrates how to define an Alpine.js Data Component using 100% BoxLang code. How it works Direct Access : The BoxLang script uses js.Alpine.data() to register a component. Normalization : The BoxLang struct returned by the component function becomes the JavaScript object that Alpine uses as the component's data. Closures : The increment , decrement and isEven functions in the struct are wrapped as JS functions that Alpine can call. Calls from HTML : The buttons in index.html call count = increment(count, step) . The BoxLang function receives the current values and returns the new count, which Alpine assigns. The component uses function( initialValue = 0 ) { ... } to provide a default initial value. Building the Example You must compile the BoxLang script into a JavaScript/WASM bundle using the MatchBox CLI. The build runs the wasm-bindgen command-line tool, so install wasm-bindgen-cli (or set the WASM_BINDGEN variable to its path) first: cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli matchbox --target js counter.bxs This produces: counter.js : The ES module entry point. index.html imports its ready and registerComponent exports. counter.wasm : The WASM binary containing the BoxLang VM and your compiled code for the browser. counter.d.ts and counter_bg.wasm.d.ts : TypeScript declarations. Running the Example Since browsers block WASM loading from file:// URIs, you must serve this folder using a local web server: # Using Python python3 -m http.server 8000 # Using Node.js (npx) npx serve . Then open http://localhost:8000 in your browser.
markdown:
This example demonstrates how to define an **Alpine.js Data Component** using 100% BoxLang code.

## How it works

1. **Direct Access** : The BoxLang script uses `js.Alpine.data()` to register a component.
2. **Normalization**: The BoxLang struct returned by the component function becomes the JavaScript object that Alpine uses as the component's data.
3. **Closures** : The `increment`, `decrement` and `isEven` functions in the struct are wrapped as JS functions that Alpine can call.
4. **Calls from HTML** : The buttons in `index.html` call `count = increment(count, step)`. The BoxLang function receives the current values and returns the new count, which Alpine assigns.

The component uses `function( initialValue = 0 ) { ... }` to provide a default initial value.

## Building the Example

You must compile the BoxLang script into a JavaScript/WASM bundle using the MatchBox CLI. The build runs the `wasm-bindgen` command-line tool, so install `wasm-bindgen-cli` (or set the `WASM_BINDGEN` variable to its path) first:

```bash
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli
matchbox --target js counter.bxs
```

This produces:

* `counter.js`: The ES module entry point. `index.html` imports its `ready` and `registerComponent` exports.
* `counter.wasm`: The WASM binary containing the BoxLang VM and your compiled code for the browser.
* `counter.d.ts` and `counter_bg.wasm.d.ts`: TypeScript declarations.

## Running the Example

Since browsers block WASM loading from `file://` URIs, you must serve this folder using a local web server:

```bash
# Using Python
python3 -m http.server 8000

# Using Node.js (npx)
npx serve .
```

Then open `http://localhost:8000` in your browser.

title: BoxLang Compatibility
body: MatchBox is an independent Rust runtime for BoxLang. It shares the language's core syntax and programming model while bringing it to native binaries, browsers, WASI hosts and ESP32 devices. Familiar language, different runtime You can use variables, strings, arrays, structs, functions, closures, classes, loops and error handling. MatchBox also provides built-in functions for common work such as JSON, dates, collections and file handling. Start with the course or browse the language reference . Choose the target for your application Target Best suited to Native CLI tools, local applications and services with access to the host system. Browser Client-side applications and libraries, using WebAssembly and JavaScript integration. WASI Experimental WebAssembly workloads outside the browser. ESP32 Embedded applications with device-specific APIs and resource limits. Native Fusion lets you add Rust code on all targets. The Rust code and its dependencies must support the chosen target. Host APIs and modules The JVM runtime has direct access to Java libraries and the broader JVM ecosystem. MatchBox uses its own host integrations and native modules. A JVM library or module may need a MatchBox backend rather than running unchanged. Modules add shared BoxLang code and optional native functionality. Java interop is experimental and is not available in the browser. Web development provides templates, routes and request scopes on server builds. Database access depends on the build and driver. The browser playground runs locally without files, networking, Java or JIT. It is useful for learning the language, not for testing every host integration. Moving an application Start with the application logic, then check its libraries and host APIs. Run a small example on the target you intend to ship, especially when moving an existing JVM application. For changes and open bugs, use the changelog and issue tracker .
markdown:
MatchBox is an independent Rust runtime for BoxLang. It shares the language's core syntax and programming model while bringing it to native binaries, browsers, WASI hosts and ESP32 devices.

## Familiar language, different runtime

You can use variables, strings, arrays, structs, functions, closures, classes, loops and error handling. MatchBox also provides built-in functions for common work such as JSON, dates, collections and file handling.

Start with the [course](/course/index.html) or browse the [language reference](/reference/language/index.html).

## Choose the target for your application

|                              Target                               |                                    Best suited to                                     |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [Native](/building-and-deploying/native-builds/index.html)        | CLI tools, local applications and services with access to the host system.            |
| [Browser](/building-and-deploying/javascript-and-wasm/index.html) | Client-side applications and libraries, using WebAssembly and JavaScript integration. |
| [WASI](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html)         | Experimental WebAssembly workloads outside the browser.                               |
| [ESP32](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html)                 | Embedded applications with device-specific APIs and resource limits.                  |

Native Fusion lets you add Rust code on all targets. The Rust code and its dependencies must support the chosen target.

## Host APIs and modules

The JVM runtime has direct access to Java libraries and the broader JVM ecosystem. MatchBox uses its own host integrations and native modules. A JVM library or module may need a MatchBox backend rather than running unchanged.

* [Modules](/reference/language/modules/index.html) add shared BoxLang code and optional native functionality.
* [Java interop](/reference/language/java-interop/index.html) is experimental and is not available in the browser.
* [Web development](/building-and-deploying/web-server/index.html) provides templates, routes and request scopes on server builds.
* [Database access](/reference/language/query-and-data/index.html) depends on the build and driver.

The browser playground runs locally without files, networking, Java or JIT. It is useful for learning the language, not for testing every host integration.

## Moving an application

Start with the application logic, then check its libraries and host APIs. Run a small example on the target you intend to ship, especially when moving an existing JVM application.

For changes and open bugs, use the [changelog](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md) and [issue tracker](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox/issues).

title: Build and ship
body: Up to now you have run source files. MatchBox can also build them into something you can ship. This lesson uses a terminal, because a browser tab cannot create files. Start with this script, saved as hello.bxs . Run it here first to be sure it works. function greet( name ) { return "Hello, #name#!"; } println( greet( "world" ) ); Output: Hello, world! A native executable matchbox --target native hello.bxs ./hello MatchBox prints Native binary produced: hello . The result is one self-contained file that contains the runtime and your compiled program. You can copy it to another machine of the same operating system and architecture and run it with no MatchBox and no JVM installed. Build on each platform you want to support, and test the result there. Bytecode matchbox --build hello.bxs matchbox hello.bxb This compiles to a .bxb file instead. Add --strip-source to leave the source text out of the file. Unlike a native executable, a .bxb needs a compatible MatchBox on the machine that runs it. Where else can it run? The same script can be built for other places. Each has its own guide: Target Guide Native executable Native builds Browser and JavaScript JavaScript and WebAssembly Containers Docker image and WASM container AWS Lambda AWS Lambda Microcontrollers ESP32 Targets differ in what they can reach. A browser build has no files or sockets, for example, and a microcontroller has far less memory. Check the guide for the target you pick. Try it Build your own script as a native executable, run it, and check that it prints the same thing as matchbox yourscript.bxs .
markdown:
Up to now you have run source files. MatchBox can also build them into something you can ship. This lesson uses a terminal, because a browser tab cannot create files.

Start with this script, saved as `hello.bxs`. Run it here first to be sure it works.

```boxlang
function greet( name ) {
    return "Hello, #name#!";
}

println( greet( "world" ) );
```

Output:

```text
Hello, world!
```

## A native executable

```sh
matchbox --target native hello.bxs
./hello
```

MatchBox prints `Native binary produced: hello`. The result is one self-contained file that contains the runtime and your compiled program. You can copy it to another machine of the same operating system and architecture and run it with no MatchBox and no JVM installed. Build on each platform you want to support, and test the result there.

## Bytecode

```sh
matchbox --build hello.bxs
matchbox hello.bxb
```

This compiles to a `.bxb` file instead. Add `--strip-source` to leave the source text out of the file. Unlike a native executable, a `.bxb` needs a compatible MatchBox on the machine that runs it.

## Where else can it run?

The same script can be built for other places. Each has its own guide:

|         Target         |                                                                  Guide                                                                  |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Native executable      | [Native builds](/building-and-deploying/native-builds/index.html)                                                                       |
| Browser and JavaScript | [JavaScript and WebAssembly](/building-and-deploying/javascript-and-wasm/index.html)                                                    |
| Containers             | [Docker image](/building-and-deploying/docker-image/index.html) and [WASM container](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html) |
| AWS Lambda             | [AWS Lambda](/building-and-deploying/aws-lambda-aws-cli-setup/index.html)                                                               |
| Microcontrollers       | [ESP32](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html)                                                                                       |

Targets differ in what they can reach. A browser build has no files or sockets, for example, and a microcontroller has far less memory. Check the guide for the target you pick.

## Try it

Build your own script as a native executable, run it, and check that it prints the same thing as `matchbox yourscript.bxs`.

title: Building for ESP32
body: matchbox --target esp32 cross-compiles the MatchBox ESP32 runner, flashes it, and writes your application to a flash partition. The standard runner is a small web application server: it starts Wi-Fi, listens for HTTP, and runs BoxLang files in response to requests. Returns { mode: "station", ip } . esp32WifiAccessPoint( ssid, [password], [channel=1] ) Starts an access point. Returns { mode: "accessPoint", ip } . esp32WifiStatus() { mode, ip } , with mode "off" and an empty ip when not connected. Commands go through a queue of eight, and each function returns true once the command is queued. An error is raised if the driver cannot be installed or the host has not mounted the device. Function Purpose esp32RegisterAsHID( [productName] ) Install the USB HID driver. esp32USBHidReady() true when the driver is installed and the host has mounted the device. esp32USBMouseMove( dx, dy ) Move the pointer. Each value from -128 to 127. esp32USBMouseClick( button ) Press and release. 1 left, 2 right, 3 middle; values 1 to 7 are accepted. esp32USBMouseDown( button ) , esp32USBMouseUp( button ) Hold and release a button. esp32USBMouseScroll( x, y ) Scroll. Each value from -128 to 127. esp32USBKeyboardPress( keycode ) , esp32USBKeyboardRelease( keycode ) Press and release a key by USB HID usage code, 0 to 255. esp32USBKeyboardReleaseAll() Release all keys. Each name also exists in the spellings esp32UsbMouseMove and esp32usbmousemove .
