Returns { id, format, imageUrl, bytes, width, height, version } . esp32CameraCaptureBitmap() Capture and convert to a monochrome bitmap { width, height, bytesPerRow, bytes } . esp32PhotoInfo( photo ) The capture struct for a stored photo. esp32PhotoUrl( photo ) /__matchbox/photo/<id>?v=<version> . esp32PhotoFree( [photo] ) Release a stored photo. esp32BitmapFromJpeg( bytes ) Convert JPEG bytes to the monochrome bitmap struct. photo is the struct returned by esp32CameraCapture() or its numeric id . BLE printer Available only in a runner built with platform-bluetooth (see above). The functions send TSPL commands over a BLE characteristic; the default characteristic is 00002af1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb . Function Purpose esp32BluetoothConnect( options ) Connect. options accepts address , addressType , namePrefix , characteristicUuid and timeoutMs (default 5000). Returns { handleId, deviceName, deviceId, writeMode, characteristicUuid } . esp32BluetoothDisconnect( handle ) Disconnect. esp32BluetoothWrite( address, characteristicUuid, payload ) Write bytes or text to a characteristic. esp32PrintTspl( payload ) Send TSPL to a printer. esp32PrintTsplTo( address, payload ) Send TSPL to a printer at an address. esp32PrinterPrintTspl( handle, payload ) Send TSPL over an open connection. esp32PrintHelloBoxLang() Print a test label. esp32PrinterCaptureBitmap( handle ) , esp32CaptureAndPrint() , esp32CaptureBitmapAndPrintTo( address, ... ) Capture a camera frame and print it. Also require the camera ( esp32s3 ). handle is the connection struct or its handleId . Troubleshooting Missing ldproxy If the runner build fails with linker ldproxy not found : cargo install ldproxy Stale build artifacts After changing ESP-IDF version, chip or shell environment, remove the runner build output and retry: rm -rf crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/target rm -rf target/esp32_stubs Manual flash If the ELF builds but the CLI cannot open the serial device, flash it with espflash : espflash flash \ --chip esp32s3 \ --port /dev/ttyACM0 \ --partition-table crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/partitions.csv \ main.elf
markdown:
`matchbox --target esp32` cross-compiles the MatchBox ESP32 runner, flashes it, and writes your application to a flash partition. The standard runner is a small web application server: it starts Wi-Fi, listens for HTTP, and runs BoxLang files in response to requests.

## What the runner executes

The runner executes only two things: the `Application` class (its `onApplicationStart` method) and the route files in the embedded app. It has no loader for a standalone script, so a file that only calls `println` and `sleep` is compiled but the device does not run it.

Routes come from an `app/` directory next to your entry script, not from `web.server()` calls. The entry script is still required on the command line. It is compiled and checked, but the routes are built from the files in `app/`.

    my-device/
    ├── main.bxs                  entry script passed to matchbox
    ├── Application.bx            optional, runs onApplicationStart at boot
    ├── box.json                  optional build settings
    └── app/
        ├── index.bxm             GET /
        ├── status.get.bxs        GET /status
        ├── print.post.bxs        POST /print
        └── printer/
            └── [id].bxm          GET /printer/:id

Route rules:

* Only `.bxm` (template) and `.bxs` (script) files under `app/` become routes.
* `index` maps to the directory path. Other names map to a path segment, so `app/about.bxm` is `/about`.
* A method suffix before the extension sets the method: `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head` or `options`. The default is `GET`.
* `[name]` in a file or directory name captures that segment as `name`.
* A route matches when the segment count is equal and each literal segment is equal. If several routes match, the first one in alphabetical path order wins.
* `Application.bx` is found next to the entry script or in `src/main/bx/`.

Each request runs the route file in a shared VM and responds as follows:

| Route file                 | Response                                               |
|:---------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `.bxm`                     | The captured output as `text/html; charset=utf-8`.     |
| `.bxs` that writes output  | The captured output as `text/html; charset=utf-8`.     |
| `.bxs` that writes nothing | Its result value serialized as `application/json`.     |
| Error while running        | `500` with `Embedded route execution failed: <error>`. |
| No route                   | `404` with `Embedded route not found`.                 |

Inside a route the scopes are strings only:

| Scope     | Contents                                                                                                   |
|:----------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `url`     | Query parameters, then route parameters (a route parameter overwrites a query parameter of the same name). |
| `form`    | Fields of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body. Other body types are not read.                      |
| `request` | Empty struct.                                                                                              |
| `cgi`     | `request_method`, `path_info` and `request_uri`.                                                           |

Not available: sessions, cookies, static files, `event.setView()`, `app.listen()`, webhooks and WebSockets. Compile-time checks on the entry script reject `app.listen()`, `event.setView()` / `event.renderTemplate()`, `app.middleware.buildStaticFiles()`, webhook helpers, cookie helpers and session helpers.

## Prerequisites

You need these on the development machine:

1. **Rust ESP32 toolchain** , installed with `espup`:

   ```sh
   cargo install espup
   espup install
   ```

2. **ESP-IDF** , a real checkout activated in your shell. MatchBox builds with `ESP_IDF_TOOLS_INSTALL_DIR=fromenv` so it uses the tools of the activated environment instead of downloading its own.
3. **espflash** for flashing.
4. **ldproxy** , the linker wrapper used by the runner:

   ```sh
   cargo install ldproxy
   ```

5. A C toolchain, Python, CMake and Ninja, as required by ESP-IDF.
6. **A MatchBox source checkout.** A build with `--esp32-web` compiles the runner from `crates/matchbox-esp32-runner` in the source tree the CLI was built from.

Activate ESP-IDF and switch the Rust toolchain in the shell you run MatchBox from:

```sh
source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh
export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp
```

Do not layer other ESP export scripts on top of that shell. Without these variables the runner build fails.

### Check your setup

```sh
matchbox esp32-doctor
```

The command prints `[ok]`, `[warning]` or `[fail]` for each of: `IDF_PATH`, `idf.py`, `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`, `cargo`, `cmake`, `ninja`, `ldproxy`, `espflash`, `LIBCLANG_PATH`, `ESP_IDF_ESPUP_CLANG_SYMLINK`, the bundled `esp32`, `esp32s3` and `esp32c3` stubs, a `.cargo/config.toml` in the current directory that forces an ESP target, and serial devices under `/dev`. It ends with a summary line and exits normally; read the `[fail]` lines.

### WSL users

Attach the USB device to the Linux instance with `usbipd-win`, from a Windows Administrator PowerShell:

```powershell
usbipd list
usbipd attach --busid <BUSID> --auto-attach
```

## Build and flash

```sh
matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --full-flash
```

| Flag              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--target esp32`  | Build for ESP32.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `--esp32-web`     | Build the routed web runner and embed the `app/` routes. Required for the `app/` model. Without it a `web.server()` call in the entry script is rejected at compile time.                                                                                                                                       |
| `--chip <name>`   | `esp32`, `esp32s2`, `esp32s3`, `esp32c3`, `esp32c6` or `esp32h2`. `esp32c3`, `esp32c6` and `esp32h2` build for `riscv32imc-esp-espidf`; the others for the matching Xtensa target. Any other value, and an omitted flag, builds for `esp32` while still passing your text to `espflash`, so check the spelling. |
| `--full-flash`    | Build the runner, flash the firmware with the project partition table, and write the app. Implies flashing.                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `--flash`         | Fast deploy: skip the firmware build and write only the app to flash.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `--watch`         | Watch mode, see below. Implies flashing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `--output <file>` | Where to write the firmware ELF. Default: the entry script with an `.elf` extension.                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

A `--esp32-web` build always compiles the runner locally with `cargo build --release --no-default-features --features embedded-web` (adding `psram` when enabled). The route table is compiled into that firmware, and the runner falls back to it when the storage partition holds no valid app. Use `--full-flash` for the first flash, after changing chip, `box.json` or MatchBox, and whenever a fast deploy does not change what the device serves.

A fast deploy compiles the routes, then writes a 4-byte little-endian length followed by the serialized route table with `espflash write-bin` and resets the board. Run it from the shell where `espflash` can open the serial port.

### Serial port permissions

On Linux the build can succeed while flashing fails because your user cannot open the serial device (for example `/dev/ttyACM0`):

```sh
groups
sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
# or the serial group of your distribution, such as uucp
```

Log out and back in before retrying. Do not rerun the whole `matchbox ... --full-flash` command with `sudo`; that repeats the build as root. Build as your user, then flash the ELF with `espflash` (see [Manual flash](#manual-flash)).

## Watch mode

```sh
matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --watch
```

1. The first deploy is a full flash.
2. The CLI detects the serial port with `espflash board-info`, falling back to `/dev/ttyACM0`, `/dev/ttyUSB0`, `/dev/ttyACM1` or `/dev/ttyUSB1`, and prints the device output by reading the port with `stty` and `cat`.
3. When the entry script file is saved, it stops the reader, recompiles, rediscovers `app/`, fast-deploys (three attempts) and restarts the reader.

Only saves of the entry script itself trigger a redeploy. Saving a file under `app/` does not; touch the entry script afterwards. Watch mode works on Unix-style systems that have `stty` and `cat`.

## Partitions

The project partition table (`crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/partitions.csv`, passed to `espflash`) assumes **8 MB of flash** (`CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_8MB`).

| Name       | Type                 | Size                     |
|:-----------|:---------------------|:-------------------------|
| `nvs`      | data, nvs            | 0x4000                   |
| `otadata`  | data, ota            | 0x2000                   |
| `phy_init` | data, phy            | 0x1000                   |
| `factory`  | app                  | 3 MiB                    |
| `coredump` | data, coredump       | 64 KiB                   |
| `storage`  | data, subtype `0x81` | 0x2F0000 (about 2.9 MiB) |

The runner finds the `storage` partition by subtype, memory-maps it, and reads the app from it. Core dumps are written to flash (`CONFIG_ESP_COREDUMP_ENABLE_TO_FLASH`).

## Runner internals

* The runner starts a FreeRTOS task named `matchbox-runner` with a **24 KiB** stack (`24576` bytes) on core 0. A project with a `native/` directory builds a Native Fusion runner instead, whose VM task has a 48 KiB stack.
* The HTTP server task stack is 6144 bytes. The background fiber thread has 8192 bytes.
* Request handling takes a garbage collection before and after each route.
* Standard BIFs such as `println` write to the serial console.

### HTTP server limits

| Setting                      | Value                                                                 |
|:-----------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `max_sessions`               | 2                                                                     |
| `max_open_sockets`           | 2                                                                     |
| `max_uri_handlers`           | 20                                                                    |
| Methods routed to your files | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`            |
| Port                         | 80 unless `webPort` or `MATCHBOX_ESP32_WEB_PORT` is set at build time |

### Built-in endpoints

These paths are served by the runner and cannot be used by routes:

| Path                                                                                                               | Response                                                                                                    |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `/__matchbox`                                                                                                      | HTML page with hostname, IP, features and route count.                                                      |
| `/__matchbox/ping`                                                                                                 | `pong` as text.                                                                                             |
| `/__matchbox/status`                                                                                               | JSON with `hostname`, `ip`, `features`, `heap`, `diagnostics`, `partitions` and `routes`.                   |
| `/__matchbox/photo/<id>`                                                                                           | The captured photo with that id (`image/jpeg`), or `404`.                                                   |
| `/generate_204`, `/gen_204`, `/hotspot-detect.html`, `/library/test/success.html`, `/connecttest.txt`, `/ncsi.txt` | `302` redirect to `http://192.168.4.1/`, for captive-portal checks when the device runs as an access point. |

## Configuration

### Wi-Fi and port

The runner's own Wi-Fi connection and its HTTP port are fixed when the firmware is built. Provide them in one of two ways:

**`box.json` in the directory where you run `matchbox`:**

```json
{
  "esp32": {
    "board": "xiao-esp32s3-sense",
    "psram": true,
    "webPort": 80,
    "wifi": {
      "ssid": "my-network",
      "password": "my-password",
      "hostname": "my-device"
    }
  }
}
```

**Environment variables** set before running `matchbox`:

| Variable                       | Equivalent      | Meaning                                                              |
|:-------------------------------|:----------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID`     | `wifi.ssid`     | Station network name.                                                |
| `MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD` | `wifi.password` | Station password.                                                    |
| `MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_HOSTNAME` | `wifi.hostname` | Device hostname. Default `matchbox-esp32`.                           |
| `MATCHBOX_ESP32_WEB_PORT`      | `webPort`       | HTTP port.                                                           |
| `MATCHBOX_ESP32_BOARD`         | `board`         | `xiao-esp32s3-sense` selects the XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense PSRAM settings. |
| `MATCHBOX_ESP32_PSRAM`         | `psram`         | Setting the variable to any value enables PSRAM.                     |

These values are read when the runner is compiled, so they apply to `--full-flash` builds, not to a fast deploy. `box.json` values are exported by the CLI for that build. Keep real credentials out of version control.

Alternatively connect from BoxLang in `Application.bx`. `onApplicationStart` runs before the runner opens its own connection, and a connection made there is reused:

    class {
        function onApplicationStart() {
            esp32WifiStation( "my-network", "my-password", "my-device" );
        }
    }

`application.esp32.wifi.ssid`, `.password`, `.hostname` and `application.esp32.web.port` are filled in before `onApplicationStart` and can be read in routes. Changing them does not reconnect Wi-Fi or move the HTTP port: the runner only prints them to the boot log.

### Features compiled into the runner

| Cargo feature                                         | Provides                                         |
|:------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| `platform-web`                                        | HTTP routing. Enabled by `embedded-web`.         |
| `platform-mdns`                                       | mDNS announcement.                               |
| `platform-bluetooth`                                  | BLE (NimBLE), required by the printer functions. |
| `platform-printer`                                    | Printer helpers, depends on bluetooth.           |
| `platform-camera`, `platform-pins`, `platform-sdcard` | Listed in the crate's default set.               |
| `psram`                                               | PSRAM support.                                   |

The CLI builds the web runner with `--no-default-features --features embedded-web`, so the BLE and printer functions below are in the firmware only when the runner is built with the `platform-bluetooth` feature, for example by running `cargo build` in the runner crate yourself.

## ESP32 functions

### Wi-Fi

| Function                                                | Returns                                                               |
|:--------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `esp32WifiStation( ssid, password, [hostname] )`        | Connects as a station. Returns `{ mode: "station", ip }`.             |
| `esp32WifiAccessPoint( ssid, [password], [channel=1] )` | Starts an access point. Returns `{ mode: "accessPoint", ip }`.        |
| `esp32WifiStatus()`                                     | `{ mode, ip }`, with mode `"off"` and an empty ip when not connected. |

### USB HID

These functions make the board act as a USB keyboard and mouse through the ESP-IDF TinyUSB driver. Calls that need the device install the driver first with the product name `MatchBox HID`; call `esp32RegisterAsHID()` first to choose another name. Commands go through a queue of eight, and each function returns `true` once the command is queued. An error is raised if the driver cannot be installed or the host has not mounted the device.

| Function                                                                 | Purpose                                                                         |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `esp32RegisterAsHID( [productName] )`                                    | Install the USB HID driver.                                                     |
| `esp32USBHidReady()`                                                     | `true` when the driver is installed and the host has mounted the device.        |
| `esp32USBMouseMove( dx, dy )`                                            | Move the pointer. Each value from -128 to 127.                                  |
| `esp32USBMouseClick( button )`                                           | Press and release. `1` left, `2` right, `3` middle; values 1 to 7 are accepted. |
| `esp32USBMouseDown( button )`, `esp32USBMouseUp( button )`               | Hold and release a button.                                                      |
| `esp32USBMouseScroll( x, y )`                                            | Scroll. Each value from -128 to 127.                                            |
| `esp32USBKeyboardPress( keycode )`, `esp32USBKeyboardRelease( keycode )` | Press and release a key by USB HID usage code, 0 to 255.                        |
| `esp32USBKeyboardReleaseAll()`                                           | Release all keys.                                                               |

Each name also exists in the spellings `esp32UsbMouseMove` and `esp32usbmousemove`.

### Camera

The camera functions are compiled in only for the `esp32s3` chip, and use the pin presets of the XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense.

| Function                       | Purpose                                                                                                  |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `esp32CameraCapture()`         | Capture a JPEG and keep it in memory. Returns `{ id, format, imageUrl, bytes, width, height, version }`. |
| `esp32CameraCaptureBitmap()`   | Capture and convert to a monochrome bitmap `{ width, height, bytesPerRow, bytes }`.                      |
| `esp32PhotoInfo( photo )`      | The capture struct for a stored photo.                                                                   |
| `esp32PhotoUrl( photo )`       | `/__matchbox/photo/<id>?v=<version>`.                                                                    |
| `esp32PhotoFree( [photo] )`    | Release a stored photo.                                                                                  |
| `esp32BitmapFromJpeg( bytes )` | Convert JPEG bytes to the monochrome bitmap struct.                                                      |

`photo` is the struct returned by `esp32CameraCapture()` or its numeric `id`.

### BLE printer

Available only in a runner built with `platform-bluetooth` (see above). The functions send TSPL commands over a BLE characteristic; the default characteristic is `00002af1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb`.

| Function                                                                                                        | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `esp32BluetoothConnect( options )`                                                                              | Connect. `options` accepts `address`, `addressType`, `namePrefix`, `characteristicUuid` and `timeoutMs` (default 5000). Returns `{ handleId, deviceName, deviceId, writeMode, characteristicUuid }`. |
| `esp32BluetoothDisconnect( handle )`                                                                            | Disconnect.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `esp32BluetoothWrite( address, characteristicUuid, payload )`                                                   | Write bytes or text to a characteristic.                                                                                                                                                             |
| `esp32PrintTspl( payload )`                                                                                     | Send TSPL to a printer.                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `esp32PrintTsplTo( address, payload )`                                                                          | Send TSPL to a printer at an address.                                                                                                                                                                |
| `esp32PrinterPrintTspl( handle, payload )`                                                                      | Send TSPL over an open connection.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `esp32PrintHelloBoxLang()`                                                                                      | Print a test label.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `esp32PrinterCaptureBitmap( handle )`, `esp32CaptureAndPrint()`, `esp32CaptureBitmapAndPrintTo( address, ... )` | Capture a camera frame and print it. Also require the camera (`esp32s3`).                                                                                                                            |

`handle` is the connection struct or its `handleId`.

## Troubleshooting

### Missing `ldproxy`

If the runner build fails with `linker ldproxy not found`:

```sh
cargo install ldproxy
```

### Stale build artifacts

After changing ESP-IDF version, chip or shell environment, remove the runner build output and retry:

```sh
rm -rf crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/target
rm -rf target/esp32_stubs
```

### Manual flash

If the ELF builds but the CLI cannot open the serial device, flash it with `espflash`:

```sh
espflash flash \
  --chip esp32s3 \
  --port /dev/ttyACM0 \
  --partition-table crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/partitions.csv \
  main.elf
```

markdown:
You do not need Rust to use a prebuilt CLI. Build from source when you want to contribute to MatchBox or customize the runtime.

## Build the CLI

Install a current stable [Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs/) and your platform's compiler and linker, then run:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox.git
cd matchbox
cargo build --release
./target/release/matchbox --version
```

On Windows, the executable is `target/release/matchbox.exe`.

## Runner stubs

The build embeds small runtimes, called runner stubs, so the CLI can package applications without downloading a runtime at build time.

Install the Rust targets for the outputs you need:

|       Rust target        |              Used for              |
|--------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `wasm32-unknown-unknown` | Browser builds with `--target js`. |
| `wasm32-wasip1`          | Experimental WASI modules.         |
| `wasm32-wasip2`          | Experimental WASI HTTP components. |

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown wasm32-wasip1 wasm32-wasip2
```

Browser packaging also needs the matching `wasm-bindgen` CLI:

```sh
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version 0.2.114 --locked
```

For additional desktop runners:

```sh
cargo build --release --features cross-compile
```

Each runner needs its platform's build tools. A target can only be packaged when its runner is available.

## Cargo features

The default CLI includes common I/O, HTTP, crypto and terminal functions, Java interop, JIT and the web server. Features let you customize source builds:

|                    Feature                    |                  Purpose                   |
|-----------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `bif-io`, `bif-http`, `bif-crypto`, `bif-cli` | Common host integrations.                  |
| `bif-jni`                                     | Java interoperability through a host JVM.  |
| `bif-datasource`, `bif-zip`                   | Database and archive functions.            |
| `server`                                      | Built-in web serving and its dependencies. |
| `jit`                                         | Cranelift JIT on supported native builds.  |
| `bif-tui`                                     | Terminal UI classes.                       |
| `qoq`                                         | Query of queries.                          |
| `cross-compile`                               | Additional desktop runner stubs.           |

For a smaller CLI without the server and its dependencies:

```sh
cargo build --release --no-default-features --features bif-io,bif-http
```

Cargo features can enable other features through dependencies. Use `cargo tree -e features` to inspect a custom build; the root `Cargo.toml` is the complete feature list.

## Browser runtime for source strings

`--target js` packages a compiled application. To compile source strings in the browser, use a small WebAssembly crate with `matchbox_compiler` and `matchbox_vm`, as this site's `playground-runtime/` does.

From the documentation repository, rebuild its runtime with:

```sh
bash tools/build-runtime.sh
npm run test:playground
```

## ESP32

ESP32 builds need the Espressif Rust toolchain, an activated ESP-IDF environment and flashing tools. Start with `matchbox esp32-doctor` and follow the [ESP32 guide](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html).

## Project layout

The main pieces are in `crates/`: the parser, compiler, VM, module system and target-specific runners. The root crate provides the CLI; `build.rs` prepares embedded runners. Tests live in `tests/`.

```sh
cargo test
cargo clippy
```

See [Native Fusion](/building-and-deploying/native-fusion/index.html) for building applications with Rust code, and [releases](/reference/releases/index.html) for published distributions.

title: Classes
body: A class groups data with the methods that work on it. Define one inside a script or in a .bx file, then create an instance with new . Constructor, this and variables init() initializes the object. Use this for public fields and variables for private instance state. Returning this also makes methods chainable. class Counter { function init( start = 0 ) { variables.count = start; return this; } function increment() { variables.count += 1; return this; } function get() { return variables.count; } } println( new Counter( 5 ).increment().increment().get() ); 7 File-based classes Put a class in a file such as models/Pet.bx : class { function init( name ) { this.name = name; return this; } function speak() { return "I am " & this.name; } } Import and use it from your application: import models.Pet; println( new Pet( "Rex" ).speak() ); File-based classes need a project filesystem; use inline classes in the browser playground. Inheritance and interfaces Use extends="Parent" to inherit behavior and implements="Interface" to declare an interface. A child can override methods and call the parent implementation with super.method() . class Animal { function speak() { return "hello"; } } class Dog extends="Animal" { function speak() { return super.speak() & " from Dog"; } } println( new Dog().speak() ); hello from Dog Properties and accessors Properties provide getter and setter methods: class Person accessors="true" { property name; } person = new Person(); person.setName( "Ann" ); println( person.getName() ); Ann For a guided introduction, see the classes lesson .

title: Classes and objects
body: A class bundles data with the functions that work on it. You create an object from a class with new . A first class class Counter { function init( start = 0 ) { variables.count = start; return this; } function increment() { variables.count = variables.count + 1; return this; } function get() { return variables.count; } } c = new Counter( 5 ); c.increment(); c.increment(); println( c.get() ); Output: 7 init is the constructor . It runs when you call new Counter( 5 ) . variables.count is private state, stored inside the object. Code outside the class reaches it only through the methods. this is the object itself. Chaining Because increment returns this , calls can be chained: class Counter { function init( start = 0 ) { variables.count = start; return this; } function increment() { variables.count = variables.count + 1; return this; } function get() { return variables.count; } } println( new Counter().increment().increment().increment().get() ); Output: 3 Public data Values you store on this are public. That is simple, but it means anyone can change them. class Account { function init( owner, balance = 0 ) { this.owner = owner; variables.balance = balance; return this; } function deposit( amount ) { variables.balance = variables.balance + amount; return this; } function withdraw( amount ) { if ( amount > variables.balance ) { throw( type = "Funds", message = "Insufficient funds" ); } variables.balance = variables.balance - amount; return this; } function getBalance() { return variables.balance; } } account = new Account( "Ada", 100 ); account.deposit( 50 ).withdraw( 30 ); println( account.owner & " has " & account.getBalance() ); try { account.withdraw( 500 ); } catch ( Funds e ) { println( "Refused: " & e.message ); } Output: Ada has 120 Refused: Insufficient funds Here the owner is public on this , while the balance is private, so the only way to change it is through deposit and withdraw , which enforce the rules. The try and catch at the bottom are the subject of the next lesson. A class that holds a collection class Stack { function init() { variables.items = []; return this; } function push( value ) { variables.items.append( value ); return this; } function pop() { return variables.items.pop(); } function size() { return variables.items.len(); } } s = new Stack().push( 1 ).push( 2 ).push( 3 ); println( s.pop() ); println( s.size() ); Output: 3 2 Going further Explore inheritance, interfaces and properties in the class reference . Try it Add a reset() method to Counter that sets the count back to zero and returns this .
headings: A class that holds a collection

markdown:
Use `matchbox` to run BoxLang, explore the REPL or package an application. Run `matchbox --help` for the options available in your installation.

```text
matchbox [options] [file or directory] [script arguments]
```

## Common commands

|               Command               |                    Purpose                     |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `matchbox`                          | Start the REPL.                                |
| `matchbox app.bxs`                  | Run a script.                                  |
| `matchbox page.bxm`                 | Run a template.                                |
| `matchbox app.bxb`                  | Run compiled bytecode.                         |
| `matchbox --eval 'println(1 + 2);'` | Run a short expression or script.              |
| `matchbox --build app.bxs`          | Write bytecode to `app.bxb`.                   |
| `matchbox --target native app.bxs`  | Build a standalone executable.                 |
| `matchbox --target js app.bxs`      | Build a browser JavaScript/WebAssembly module. |
| `matchbox --serve --webroot www`    | Serve templates and static files.              |
| `matchbox --version`                | Show the version and build information.        |

## Options

Put MatchBox options **before** the file or directory. Arguments after it belong to your script.

|         Option          |                      Purpose                      |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `-h`, `--help`          | Show usage.                                       |
| `-v`, `--version`       | Show build information.                           |
| `-e`, `--eval <source>` | Execute inline BoxLang code.                      |
| `--build`               | Compile to bytecode instead of running.           |
| `--target <target>`     | Package for a deployment target.                  |
| `--output <path>`       | Choose the output path.                           |
| `--strip-source`        | Omit embedded source text from the output.        |
| `--module <dir>`        | Load a module directory; repeat for more modules. |
| `--keep <a,b,c>`        | Keep named prelude functions during tree-shaking. |
| `--no-shaking`          | Include the full prelude.                         |
| `--no-std-lib`          | Omit the prelude.                                 |
| `--verbose`             | Enable additional build logging.                  |

For example:

```sh
mkdir -p dist
matchbox --build --strip-source --output dist/app.bxb app.bxs
```

Tree-shaking removes unused functions from the BoxLang-written standard library. `--strip-source` reduces diagnostic context; it is not encryption.

## Targets

|        Target        |                           Output                            |                                            Guide                                            |
|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `native`             | Executable for the current host.                            | [Native builds](/building-and-deploying/native-builds/index.html)                           |
| A Rust target triple | Executable using an embedded runner for that platform.      | [Cross-compilation](/building-and-deploying/native-builds/index.html#build-for-other-hosts) |
| `js`                 | JavaScript module, WebAssembly and TypeScript declarations. | [JavaScript and WebAssembly](/building-and-deploying/javascript-and-wasm/index.html)        |
| `wasi`, `wasm`       | Experimental WASI module.                                   | [WASI deployment](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html)                        |
| `wasi-http`          | Experimental HTTP component built from a webroot.           | [WASI HTTP](/building-and-deploying/wasi-http/index.html)                                   |
| `esp32`              | Device firmware or a flash operation.                       | [ESP32](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html)                                           |

Package from source (`.bxs` or `.bxm`); a `.bxb` is already compiled and is run directly. Native Fusion adds Rust code to target builds and requires the corresponding toolchain.

### WASI targets

WASI is experimental. Use `--target wasi` for a script and `--target wasi-http --webroot www` for a web application. Browser applications use `--target js`, not WASI.

## Running code

### Files and directories

A source file is compiled in memory and run. A `.bxb` file runs precompiled bytecode. Given a directory, MatchBox looks for `index.bxs`, `main.bxs` or `Application.bx`.

### Script arguments

Read script arguments with `cliGetArgs()`:

```sh
matchbox app.bxs first second --name=bob --flag
```

The result contains `positionals` and `options`. Use `--name=value` for a named value and `--flag` for a boolean option. Standalone executables receive script arguments directly.

### REPL

Start `matchbox` without a file:

```text
bx> x = 1 + 2
=> 3
bx> println(x)
3
```

The REPL reads one line at a time. Type `exit` or `quit`, or press Ctrl+D, to leave.

## Server

```sh
matchbox --serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --webroot www
```

The defaults are host `127.0.0.1`, port `8080` and the current directory as webroot. Use `0.0.0.0` to accept connections from other machines. See [Web server](/building-and-deploying/web-server/index.html) for configuration and routing.

## ESP32

```sh
matchbox esp32-doctor
matchbox --target esp32 --chip esp32s3 --full-flash main.bxs
```

`--flash` updates the application, `--full-flash` writes the firmware, and `--watch` rebuilds and flashes on changes. Use `--esp32-web` for the routed web runner. See the [ESP32 guide](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html) for setup and device requirements.

## AWS Lambda

```sh
matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json
matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx --function hello --bootstrap /path/to/bootstrap
```

Deployment uses the AWS CLI. `--public` creates an unauthenticated function URL; `--url` uses IAM authentication. See the [Lambda guide](/building-and-deploying/aws-lambda-aws-cli-setup/index.html) for roles, regions and packaging.

## Environment variables

|     Variable     |                 Purpose                 |
|------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| `WASM_BINDGEN`   | Path to the `wasm-bindgen` executable.  |
| `BOXLANG_HOME`   | Runtime home, including shared modules. |
| `MATCHBOX_DEBUG` | Compiler and tree-shaking diagnostics.  |
| `BX_TRACE`       | Detailed VM instruction tracing.        |

Scripts read environment variables with `getSystemSetting("NAME", "default")`. Project settings belong in [configuration files](/reference/configuration/index.html).

## Exit codes

Successful execution returns `0`; an unhandled script or CLI error returns `1`. Scripts can set their own exit code with `cliExit(n)`. Diagnostic commands such as `esp32-doctor` also print findings, so read their output rather than relying only on an exit code.

title: Configuration
body: Run MatchBox from your project directory so relative paths and project settings resolve together. File or directory Purpose box.json Package dependencies and ESP32 build settings. boxlang.json Runtime settings, including module configuration. matchbox.toml Explicit module paths and datasources. boxlang_modules/ Project-local modules. BOXLANG_HOME/modules/ Shared modules in the runtime home. Command-line options override the relevant settings for a run. See the CLI reference for commands and environment variables . Modules Install modules in boxlang_modules/ , or select a directory explicitly: matchbox --module ./libs/greeter app.bxs A module contains ModuleConfig.bx and can provide BoxLang code, settings and native functionality. Configure application-specific settings in boxlang.json : { "modules": { "greeter": { "settings": { "greeting": "Howdy" } } } } See Modules for the package layout and lifecycle. matchbox.toml Use explicit module paths and datasource settings when needed: [modules.greeter] path = "./libs/greeter" [datasources.main] driver = "sqlite" database = "app.db" Database support depends on the runtime build. See Queries and data for programmatic configuration and queries. ESP32 settings The esp32 block in box.json configures the device build: { "esp32": { "board": "xiao-esp32s3-sense", "psram": true, "webPort": 8080, "wifi": { "ssid": "my-network", "password": "my-password", "hostname": "matchbox-device" } } } These settings are compiled into firmware. Keep real credentials out of source control. See the ESP32 guide for toolchains and flashing. Cargo features Cargo features apply when building MatchBox itself, not as application settings. See Building MatchBox .
markdown:
Run MatchBox from your project directory so relative paths and project settings resolve together.

|    File or directory    |                      Purpose                      |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `box.json`              | Package dependencies and ESP32 build settings.    |
| `boxlang.json`          | Runtime settings, including module configuration. |
| `matchbox.toml`         | Explicit module paths and datasources.            |
| `boxlang_modules/`      | Project-local modules.                            |
| `BOXLANG_HOME/modules/` | Shared modules in the runtime home.               |

Command-line options override the relevant settings for a run. See the [CLI reference](/reference/cli/index.html) for commands and [environment variables](/reference/cli/index.html#environment-variables).

## Modules

Install modules in `boxlang_modules/`, or select a directory explicitly:

```sh
matchbox --module ./libs/greeter app.bxs
```

A module contains `ModuleConfig.bx` and can provide BoxLang code, settings and native functionality. Configure application-specific settings in `boxlang.json`:

```json
{
  "modules": {
    "greeter": {
      "settings": { "greeting": "Howdy" }
    }
  }
}
```

See [Modules](/reference/language/modules/index.html) for the package layout and lifecycle.

## matchbox.toml

Use explicit module paths and datasource settings when needed:

```toml
[modules.greeter]
path = "./libs/greeter"

[datasources.main]
driver = "sqlite"
database = "app.db"
```

Database support depends on the runtime build. See [Queries and data](/reference/language/query-and-data/index.html) for programmatic configuration and queries.

## ESP32 settings

The `esp32` block in `box.json` configures the device build:

```json
{
  "esp32": {
    "board": "xiao-esp32s3-sense",
    "psram": true,
    "webPort": 8080,
    "wifi": {
      "ssid": "my-network",
      "password": "my-password",
      "hostname": "matchbox-device"
    }
  }
}
```

These settings are compiled into firmware. Keep real credentials out of source control. See the [ESP32 guide](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html) for toolchains and flashing.

## Cargo features

Cargo features apply when building MatchBox itself, not as application settings. See [Building MatchBox](/getting-started/building-matchbox/index.html#cargo-features).

title: Destructuring, spread and ranges
body: Destructuring extracts values, spread expands collections, and ranges describe sequences for iteration. Destructuring Pull values out of a struct or an array in one statement. { name, age } = { name: "Ann", age: 30 }; println( name & " is " & age ); { name: who } = { name: "Bob" }; println( who ); [ first, second ] = [ 10, 20, 30 ]; println( first & "," & second ); { a, b } = { a: 1 }; println( isNull( b ) ); Output: Ann is 30 Bob 10,20 true A struct pattern matches by key. { name: who } renames. A key that is missing from the struct leaves the variable null. Destructuring works inside functions too. Use ...rest to collect remaining values: [ first, ...rest ] = [ 10, 20, 30 ]; println( first ); println( serializeJSON( rest ) ); 10 [20,30] Spread ... expands an array into an array literal or a call, and a struct into a struct literal. base = [ 1, 2 ]; println( serializeJSON( [ 0, ...base, 3 ] ) ); println( serializeJSON( [ ...base, ...base ] ) ); defaults = { color: "red" }; println( serializeJSON( { ...defaults, size: 9 } ) ); function add( p, q ) { return p + q; } println( add( ...[ 3, 4 ] ) ); Output: [0,1,2,3] [1,2,1,2] {"color":"red","size":9} 7 To override existing struct keys, use structAppend rather than spreading a duplicate key into a literal: merged = duplicate( defaults ); structAppend( merged, { color: "blue" } ); Ranges a..b is an inclusive range and a..<b stops before b . Both are meant for for ... in . for ( i in 1..3 ) { println( "up " & i ); } for ( i in 3..1 ) { println( "down " & i ); } for ( i in 1..<4 ) { println( "short " & i ); } n = 3; for ( i in 1..n ) { println( "var " & i ); } total = 0; for ( i in 1..100 ) { total += i; } println( total ); Output: up 1 up 2 up 3 down 3 down 2 down 1 short 1 short 2 short 3 var 1 var 2 var 3 5050 Ranges are useful in loops; use arraySlice( array, start, length ) for a portion of an array. If an exclusive range might be empty, check the bounds before iterating. See also operators and sets .

CI Example Use the image in a CI job when you only need the MatchBox CLI: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --build src/main.bxs docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --target native src/main.bxs For production and repeatable CI, pin a stable version tag or an image digest instead of latest . markdown:
MatchBox publishes a general-purpose Docker image to GitHub Container Registry:

```bash
ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox
```

The image supports Linux `amd64` and `arm64`. CI packages the same full CLI binaries published in GitHub releases using `Dockerfile.release`; the original `Dockerfile` remains available for local source builds.

The image runs the main `matchbox` CLI as its entrypoint. That makes it useful for CI builds, direct script execution, bytecode compilation, native executable generation, and webroot serving without installing MatchBox on the host.

---

## Tags

Stable releases publish:

| Tag      | Description                                                  |
|:---------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `latest` | Most recent stable release                                   |
| `vX.Y.Z` | Specific release version, matching the Git tag/Cargo version |

Develop snapshots publish:

| Tag               | Description                                        |
|:------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| `vX.Y.Z-snapshot` | Refreshed snapshot image for the next base version |
| `develop`         | Latest build from the `develop` branch             |
| `snapshot`        | Rolling snapshot alias                             |
| `be`              | Rolling BE/development image alias                 |

Pull the stable image:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest
```

Pull the current develop image:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:develop
```

---

## Basic Usage

The container workdir is `/app`. Mount your project there and pass normal MatchBox arguments:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --help
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --version
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest my_script.bxs
```

Because `matchbox` is the entrypoint, arguments after the image name are passed directly to MatchBox. Docker selects the matching image architecture automatically; use `--platform linux/amd64` or `--platform linux/arm64` when selecting it explicitly.

Use `--version` or the image's version label to identify a build. See [releases and downloads](/reference/releases/index.html) for stable and snapshot channels.

---

## Build Artifacts

Compile bytecode into the mounted project directory:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --build my_script.bxs
```

Build a native Linux artifact:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --target native my_app.bxs
```

Native artifacts produced inside the container target Linux. Use the release binaries or source builds when you need macOS or Windows native artifacts.

The image holds only the CLI binary and CA certificates (see `Dockerfile.release`). It has no Rust toolchain and no `wasm-bindgen`, so `--target js` and Native Fusion builds (a `native/` directory) cannot run inside it. WASI targets are [experimental](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html).

---

## Webroot Server

To serve `.bxm` templates and static files, bind the server to `0.0.0.0` inside the container and publish the port:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v "$PWD/www:/app" \
  ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest \
  --serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --webroot /app
```

Then open `http://localhost:8080`.

---

## CI Example

Use the image in a CI job when you only need the MatchBox CLI:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --build src/main.bxs
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --target native src/main.bxs
```

For production and repeatable CI, pin a stable version tag or an image digest instead of `latest`. Snapshot tags, including `vX.Y.Z-snapshot`, are mutable and are not immutable build pins.

title: Error handling
body: Use try and catch to handle errors, and finally for cleanup. The errors lesson introduces the basics. try, catch, finally try { throw( type = "MyError", message = "boom", detail = "more", errorCode = "E1" ); } catch ( any e ) { println( e.type & " | " & e.message & " | " & e.detail & " | " & e.errorCode ); } finally { println( "finally runs" ); } try { x = 1 / 0; } catch ( any e ) { println( e.type & ": " & e.message ); } try { throw "plain text"; } catch ( any e ) { println( e.message ); } try { try { throw "inner"; } catch ( any e ) { rethrow; } } catch ( any e ) { println( "outer got " & e.message ); } function f() { try { return "from try"; } finally { println( "cleanup" ); } } println( f() ); Output: MyError | boom | more | E1 finally runs ExpressionException: Division by zero plain text outer got inner cleanup from try The caught value is a struct. It holds only what throw was given, plus stackTrace . throw( type = "A" ) gives e.message as null, and structKeyExists( e, "type" ) is false for throw( message = "x" ) . Errors raised by the VM have e.type set to ExpressionException , for example division by zero or calling an undefined function. catch ( e ) without the any keyword is accepted. An uncaught error prints Error: ... with the source line and the CLI exits with status 1. Typed catches The first matching catch runs. Types are case-insensitive: Custom also matches Custom.Input , but not CustomInput . Use any as a fallback. Errors with no matching catch propagate outward, after finally runs. try { throw( type = "Custom.Input", message = "bad value" ); } catch ( Other e ) { println( "wrong handler" ); } catch ( "custom" e ) { println( e.message ); } catch ( any e ) { println( "fallback" ); } bad value You can also inspect e.type inside a catch when handling several cases together. function risky( kind ) { throw( type = kind, message = "failed: " & kind ); } for ( kind in [ "NotFound", "Denied", "Other" ] ) { try { risky( kind ); } catch ( any e ) { if ( e.type == "NotFound" ) { println( "404 " & e.message ); } else if ( e.type == "Denied" ) { println( "403 " & e.message ); } else { println( "unhandled " & e.type ); } } } Output: 404 failed: NotFound 403 failed: Denied unhandled Other Asynchronous errors An error inside a runAsync callback surfaces when you call get() . See async and futures .

title: Errors and control flow
body: Choosing a path temperature = 22; if ( temperature > 30 ) { println( "hot" ); } else if ( temperature > 15 ) { println( "pleasant" ); } else { println( "cold" ); } day = 3; switch ( day ) { case 1: println( "Monday" ); break; case 3: println( "Wednesday" ); break; default: println( "some other day" ); } Output: pleasant Wednesday switch needs a break at the end of each case, otherwise execution falls through into the next one. Skipping and stopping continue skips to the next round of a loop, and break leaves the loop. for ( i = 1; i <= 6; i++ ) { if ( i == 2 ) { continue; } if ( i == 5 ) { break; } println( i ); } Output: 1 3 4 Handling errors When something goes wrong, code throws an error. If nothing catches it, the script stops. A try block lets you catch the error and carry on. try { println( "before" ); throw "something broke"; println( "never printed" ); } catch ( any e ) { println( "caught: " & e.message ); } finally { println( "always runs" ); } Output: before caught: something broke always runs catch ( any e ) catches every kind of error. finally runs whether or not an error happened, which makes it the right place for cleanup. Built-in errors The runtime throws errors of its own, for example when you divide by zero. try { println( 10 / 0 ); } catch ( any e ) { println( "caught: " & e.message ); } Output: caught: Division by zero Your own error types Give an error a type so callers can catch exactly the problems they know how to handle. function parseAge( text ) { if ( !isNumeric( text ) ) { throw( type = "BadInput", message = "'" & text & "' is not a number" ); } return text + 0; } try { println( parseAge( "36" ) ); println( parseAge( "old" ) ); } catch ( BadInput e ) { println( e.type & ": " & e.message ); } Output: 36 BadInput: 'old' is not a number Try it Change the second call to parseAge( "42" ) and run again. Then add a catch ( any e ) after the BadInput one and throw a different kind of error to see which handler runs.

title: ESP32 Camera Streamer
body: This example shows a BoxLang script calling native Rust functions for cameraInit() , cameraTake() , and serialWrite() . The script sends ten byte arrays over the serial interface. [!warning] Camera capture is simulated The current Rust implementation does not initialize an ESP32 camera or capture real frames. cameraInit() reports simulated success, and cameraTake() returns a fixed ten-byte sample. Only serialWrite() writes the supplied bytes to UART0. The example is useful for exploring how a Rust runner can register native BIFs for BoxLang code. It is not a working camera firmware project. Build A native/ directory next to the entry script makes MatchBox build a Native Fusion runner for the board. That runner executes the compiled script directly instead of serving routes: source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --chip esp32s3 --full-flash The native code calls esp_idf_sys , so the project needs the ESP toolchain from the ESP32 guide . That guide also covers the routed app model and the real camera functions ( esp32CameraCapture() on esp32s3 ). For a project that serves pages, start from the regular ESP32 example .
markdown:
This example shows a BoxLang script calling native Rust functions for `cameraInit()`, `cameraTake()`, and `serialWrite()`. The script sends ten byte arrays over the serial interface.
> \[!warning\] Camera capture is simulated
> The current Rust implementation does not initialize an ESP32 camera or capture real frames. `cameraInit()` reports simulated success, and `cameraTake()` returns a fixed ten-byte sample. Only `serialWrite()` writes the supplied bytes to UART0.

The example is useful for exploring how a Rust runner can register native BIFs for BoxLang code. It is not a working camera firmware project.

## Build

A `native/` directory next to the entry script makes MatchBox build a Native Fusion runner for the board. That runner executes the compiled script directly instead of serving routes:

```sh
source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh
export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp
matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --chip esp32s3 --full-flash
```

The native code calls `esp_idf_sys`, so the project needs the ESP toolchain from the [ESP32 guide](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html). That guide also covers the routed app model and the real camera functions (`esp32CameraCapture()` on `esp32s3`). For a project that serves pages, start from the [regular ESP32 example](/examples/esp32/README/index.html).

title: ESP32 example
body: This example is a small web app for an ESP32 board. The device joins Wi-Fi and serves the files under app/ . esp32/ ├── main.bxs entry script passed to matchbox ├── Application.bx runs onApplicationStart at boot └── app/ ├── index.bxm GET / ├── hello/[name].bxm GET /hello/:name └── echo.post.bxs POST /echo The ESP32 runner does not run standalone scripts. It runs Application.bx and the route files in app/ . main.bxs is only the entry point for the command line. See Building for ESP32 for the full model. Run it Connect the board over USB and note its chip ( esp32 , esp32s3 , esp32c3 , ...). Activate ESP-IDF and the Rust ESP toolchain in your shell: source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp matchbox esp32-doctor Set your Wi-Fi network for the build, then build and flash from this directory: export MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID="my-network" export MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD="my-password" matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --full-flash You can put the same values in a box.json in this directory instead; see the guide. Watch the serial output and wait for the line that prints the address of the HTTP server: espflash monitor Open the address in a browser, or use curl: curl http://<device-ip>/ curl http://<device-ip>/hello/ESP32 curl -d "msg=hi" http://<device-ip>/echo curl http://<device-ip>/__matchbox/status /__matchbox/status is served by the runner and reports heap, partitions and the list of routes, which is a quick way to confirm which app is on the device. Change the app Edit a file under app/ and run the same command again with --flash instead of --full-flash to write only the app. If the device keeps serving the old pages, repeat with --full-flash . With --watch in place of --full-flash , saving main.bxs redeploys the app. Saving a file under app/ does not trigger a redeploy on its own.
markdown:
This example is a small web app for an ESP32 board. The device joins Wi-Fi and serves the files under `app/`.

    esp32/
    ├── main.bxs               entry script passed to matchbox
    ├── Application.bx         runs onApplicationStart at boot
    └── app/
        ├── index.bxm          GET /
        ├── hello/[name].bxm   GET /hello/:name
        └── echo.post.bxs      POST /echo

The ESP32 runner does not run standalone scripts. It runs `Application.bx` and the route files in `app/`. `main.bxs` is only the entry point for the command line. See [Building for ESP32](/building-and-deploying/esp32/index.html) for the full model.

## Run it

1. Connect the board over USB and note its chip (`esp32`, `esp32s3`, `esp32c3`, ...).
2. Activate ESP-IDF and the Rust ESP toolchain in your shell:

   ```sh
   source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh
   export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp
   matchbox esp32-doctor
   ```

3. Set your Wi-Fi network for the build, then build and flash from this directory:

   ```sh
   export MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID="my-network"
   export MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD="my-password"
   matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --full-flash
   ```

   You can put the same values in a `box.json` in this directory instead; see the guide.
4. Watch the serial output and wait for the line that prints the address of the HTTP server:

   ```sh
   espflash monitor
   ```

5. Open the address in a browser, or use curl:

   ```sh
   curl http://<device-ip>/
   curl http://<device-ip>/hello/ESP32
   curl -d "msg=hi" http://<device-ip>/echo
   curl http://<device-ip>/__matchbox/status
   ```

`/__matchbox/status` is served by the runner and reports heap, partitions and the list of routes, which is a quick way to confirm which app is on the device.

## Change the app

Edit a file under `app/` and run the same command again with `--flash` instead of `--full-flash` to write only the app. If the device keeps serving the old pages, repeat with `--full-flash`.

With `--watch` in place of `--full-flash`, saving `main.bxs` redeploys the app. Saving a file under `app/` does not trigger a redeploy on its own.

title: Functions and callbacks
body: Functions function greet( name, greeting = "Hello" ) { return greeting & ", " & name; } println( greet( "Ada" ) ); println( greet( "Ada", "Hi" ) ); println( greet( greeting = "Hey", name = "Linus" ) ); Output: Hello, Ada Hi, Ada Hey, Linus A parameter with = has a default. You can also pass arguments by name , in any order. Functions can call themselves: function factorial( n ) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial( n - 1 ); } println( factorial( 10 ) ); Output: 3628800 Arrow functions An arrow function is a short, nameless function. It is often passed to another function. double = n => n * 2; add = ( a, b ) => a + b; println( double( 4 ) ); println( add( 2, 3 ) ); Output: 8 5 Map, filter and reduce Arrays come with three workhorses. map transforms every item, filter keeps some of them, and reduce folds the array down to one value. words = [ "box", "lang", "match" ]; println( words.map( w => w.ucase() ).toList( " " ) ); println( words.filter( w => w.len() > 3 ).toList( "," ) ); println( words.reduce( ( total, w ) => total + w.len(), 0 ) ); nums = [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 ]; sumOfSquares = nums .filter( n => n % 2 == 0 ) .map( n => n * n ) .reduce( ( a, n ) => a + n, 0 ); println( sumOfSquares ); Output: BOX LANG MATCH lang,match 12 56 each , every and some work the same way. every is true when the callback is true for all items, some when it is true for at least one. println( [ 1, 2, 3 ].every( n => n > 0 ) ); println( [ 1, 2, 3 ].some( n => n > 2 ) ); [ "a", "b" ].each( v => println( "item " & v ) ); Output: true true item a item b Functions as values A function is a value, so you can pass one to another function. function apply( fn, value ) { return fn( value ); } println( apply( s => s.ucase(), "shout" ) ); println( apply( n => n + 1, 41 ) ); Output: SHOUT 42 Try it Write an arrow function isLong that returns true for words longer than 4 letters, then use it with filter on the words array.

title: HTTP requests
body: Native MatchBox includes http() when built with the bif-http feature (enabled by default). Requests run in-process; no curl executable or shell is needed. This also works in standalone native binaries . Make a Request http() returns a future. Call .get() to wait for completion, then deserialize its JSON result: response = jsonDeserialize(http({ url: "https://example.com/", timeout: 10 }).get()); println(response.status); println(response.body); The response contains: Field Meaning status Numeric HTTP status, such as 200 or 404 . body Response text, when not downloading to a file. file_content The same response text as body . file_path Destination path, when downloading to a file instead of returning text. For a JSON API, deserialize response.body separately to obtain the API's data. HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses are returned normally; check status before using the body or downloaded file. Request Options Pass a struct with these case-insensitive keys: Option Default Behavior url Required HTTP or HTTPS URL. method "GET" GET , POST , PUT , or DELETE ; case-insensitive. headers None Struct of header names and values. body None Request body as text. markdown:
Native MatchBox includes `http()` when built with the `bif-http` feature (enabled by default). Requests run in-process; no curl executable or shell is needed. This also works in [standalone native binaries](/building-and-deploying/native-builds/index.html).

## Make a Request

`http()` returns a future. Call `.get()` to wait for completion, then deserialize its JSON result:

```boxlang
response = jsonDeserialize(http({
    url: "https://example.com/",
    timeout: 10
}).get());
println(response.status);
println(response.body);
```

The response contains:

| Field          | Meaning                                                                 |
|:---------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `status`       | Numeric HTTP status, such as `200` or `404`.                            |
| `body`         | Response text, when not downloading to a file.                          |
| `file_content` | The same response text as `body`.                                       |
| `file_path`    | Destination path, when downloading to a file instead of returning text. |

For a JSON API, deserialize `response.body` separately to obtain the API's data. HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses are returned normally; check `status` before using the body or downloaded file.

## Request Options

Pass a struct with these case-insensitive keys:

| Option              | Default  | Behavior                                                                                                                                        |
|:--------------------|:---------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `url`               | Required | HTTP or HTTPS URL.                                                                                                                              |
| `method`            | `"GET"`  | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, or `DELETE`; case-insensitive.                                                                                            |
| `headers`           | None     | Struct of header names and values.                                                                                                              |
| `body`              | None     | Request body as text. Serialize JSON explicitly when needed.                                                                                    |
| `path`              | None     | Write the response body to this file instead of returning text.                                                                                 |
| `timeout`           | `30`     | Total network request deadline in **seconds** , including connection, redirects, and response-body reads/downloads. `0` disables this deadline. |
| `connectionTimeout` | `0`      | Connection deadline in **seconds** , including DNS, TCP, and TLS setup. `0` means no separate connection deadline; `timeout` still applies.     |
| `redirect`          | `true`   | Follow at most 10 redirects. `false` returns the original 3xx response without requesting its target.                                           |
| `noProxy`           | `false`  | `true` bypasses system/environment proxies for this request only. Otherwise normal proxy settings apply.                                        |
| `ipv4Only`          | `false`  | `true` restricts outgoing connections to IPv4, including connections made after redirects. Otherwise normal IPv4/IPv6 selection applies.        |

Both deadlines accept non-negative finite numbers, including fractional seconds. Negative, non-numeric, infinite, NaN, or out-of-range durations are rejected. The three boolean controls require actual `true`/`false` values, not strings or numbers. Explicit `null` is invalid for these five controls; omit a key to use its default.

The total deadline is **not** an inactivity timeout: receiving another chunk does not restart it. If both deadlines are enabled, whichever expires first ends the request.

`ipv4Only` controls this machine's connections. When using a proxy, the proxy chooses its own upstream route. Combine `ipv4Only: true` with `noProxy: true` when you need a direct IPv4 connection.

## Probe a Private Service

With `apiKey` loaded from your application's configuration:

```boxlang
try {
    response = jsonDeserialize(http({
        url: "http://private-agent:8642/api/sessions?limit=1",
        headers: { Authorization: "Bearer " & apiKey },
        timeout: 5,
        connectionTimeout: 2,
        redirect: false,
        noProxy: true,
        ipv4Only: true
    }).get());
    println("HTTP status: " & response.status);
} catch (any error) {
    println("Probe failed: " & error.message);
}
```

Headers stay in-process rather than being passed to a child command's arguments. Avoid logging request structs, credentials, or sensitive response bodies. HTTPS certificate verification remains enabled; these options do not disable TLS checks.

## Downloads and Failures

```boxlang
response = jsonDeserialize(http({
    url: "https://example.com/archive.zip",
    path: "archive.zip.tmp",
    timeout: 60
}).get());
```

A download overwrites an existing destination once response headers arrive. An interrupted download can leave a partial file. Use a temporary destination, check the status and any required checksum, and only then move it into place.

Invalid control values throw immediately from `http()`, before a connection is opened or the destination is touched. Transport and file errors reject the future and throw when `.get()` is called. Timeouts report `HTTP request timed out`. Transport diagnostics omit the request URL and do not include header values or request bodies.

The positional forms remain available with default controls: `http(url)`, `http(url, method)`, and `http(url, method, path)`. Use the struct form to configure headers, body, or request controls.

## Runtime Compatibility

This page describes **native MatchBox** , not the JVM HTTP client or browser fetch. MatchBox's request struct, future, and JSON result are distinct from JVM BoxLang's fluent HTTP client. The `timeout`, `connectionTimeout`, and `redirect` names follow BoxLang terminology; `noProxy` and `ipv4Only` are native MatchBox extensions. Do not assume these examples are drop-in JVM code.

Successful HTTP future completion is not implemented for WASM/browser builds. These options do not add WASM HTTP support. See [Differences from BoxLang](/differences-from-boxlang/index.html).

markdown:
The browser is great for learning, but real projects live on your machine. This lesson installs MatchBox and runs the same script from a terminal.

## Install with MVM

MVM is the MatchBox Version Manager. It installs releases side by side and switches between them. On Linux and macOS:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox-quick-installer/main/install/install.sh | bash
```

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox-quick-installer/main/install/install.ps1 | iex
```

Restart your shell, then install and activate the latest MatchBox:

```sh
mvm install latest
mvm use latest
matchbox --version
```

The last command prints the installed version and build information. If `matchbox` is not found, run `mvm doctor`. The [installation page](/getting-started/installation/index.html) covers other options.

## Run a script

Save this as `hello.bxs`. Press **Run** to try it here first.

```boxlang
function greet( name ) {
    return "Hello, #name#!";
}

println( greet( "world" ) );
```

Output:

```text
Hello, world!
```

Then run it from your terminal:

```sh
matchbox hello.bxs
```

MatchBox parses the file, compiles it to bytecode and runs it, all in one step.

## Compile to bytecode

You can compile once and run the result many times:

```sh
matchbox --build hello.bxs
matchbox hello.bxb
```

A `.bxb` file holds compiled bytecode. It is not a standalone program, so the machine that runs it needs a MatchBox of a compatible version. Lesson 9 shows how to build something that needs no install at all.

## Try it

Run `matchbox --version`, then run your own script. If you get stuck, the [quick start](/getting-started/quick-start/index.html) walks through the same steps.

title: Java interop
body: Native MatchBox can call Java classes through an experimental JNI bridge. This path needs a JDK on the host and a runtime built with bif-jni ; it is not available in the browser. Calling a class Use a java: import to refer to a Java class: import java:java.util.ArrayList as List; items = new List(); items.add( "hello" ); items.add( "MatchBox" ); println( items.size() ); 2 Java collection indexes follow Java's rules, so they start at 0 rather than BoxLang's 1. Choosing an integration The bridge is useful for accessing host libraries, but MatchBox is not a JVM implementation. Check the methods and runtime dependencies your application uses. A MatchBox-compatible module can also provide a native backend for selected Java-facing APIs. For Rust code owned by your application, use Native Fusion . See the Java interop example for a complete project. A standalone executable needs the same required integration support as the CLI that runs it.
markdown:
Native MatchBox can call Java classes through an experimental JNI bridge. This path needs a JDK on the host and a runtime built with `bif-jni`; it is not available in the browser.

## Calling a class

Use a `java:` import to refer to a Java class:

```boxlang
import java:java.util.ArrayList as List;

items = new List();
items.add( "hello" );
items.add( "MatchBox" );
println( items.size() );
```

```text
2
```

Java collection indexes follow Java's rules, so they start at 0 rather than BoxLang's 1.

## Choosing an integration

The bridge is useful for accessing host libraries, but MatchBox is not a JVM implementation. Check the methods and runtime dependencies your application uses.

A MatchBox-compatible module can also provide a native backend for selected Java-facing APIs. For Rust code owned by your application, use [Native Fusion](/building-and-deploying/native-fusion/index.html).

See the [Java interop example](/examples/java_interop/README/index.html) for a complete project. A standalone executable needs the same required integration support as the CLI that runs it.

title: Java interop example
body: This example uses the experimental JNI bridge to call StringBuilder , ArrayList , HashMap and Math . Run it Install a JDK and use a MatchBox CLI with JNI support. From this directory: matchbox main.bxs The script prints a greeting, collection values and results from Java's math functions. Calling Java import java:java.util.ArrayList as List; items = new List(); items.add( "hello" ); println( items.get( 0 ) ); math = createObject( "java", "java.lang.Math" ); println( math.sqrt( 144 ) ); Java collection indexes start at 0. Use createObject(...).init() when explicitly constructing an instance through a class reference. JNI is a native host integration, not a browser feature. A standalone executable also needs JNI support in its runner; ordinary runner stubs do not include it. See Java interop for the integration overview.
