markdown:
Use `--target js` to package a BoxLang application or library for the browser.

| Mode                         | Command                           | Status                                                                                                  |
|:-----------------------------|:----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **JS module (AOT)**          | `--target js`                     | Works. Ship a compiled app or library as an ES module.                                                  |
| **WASI (experimental)**      | `--target wasi` / `--target wasm` | For WASI hosts, not browsers. See [WASI deployment](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html). |
| **Runtime (source strings)** | your own crate                    | Needs a small Rust crate, described below.                                                              |

---

## Mode 1: JavaScript ES module (AOT)

MatchBox compiles your script to bytecode and writes an ES module that loads a generic MatchBox runtime (`.wasm`) and the bytecode.

### Prerequisites

The `wasm-bindgen` command line tool, version 0.2.114, must be on `PATH`, or its location set in `WASM_BINDGEN`. Without it the command stops with `wasm-bindgen not found. Install wasm-bindgen-cli or set WASM_BINDGEN.`

### Compile

```bash
matchbox --target js my_lib.bxs
```

```text
Standalone JS module produced: ./my_lib.js
```

The command writes four files next to the script, or next to `--output`:

| File                                 | Contents                                                                   |
|:-------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `my_lib.js`                          | The ES module. The compiled bytecode is embedded in it as a base64 string. |
| `my_lib.wasm`                        | The MatchBox runtime.                                                      |
| `my_lib.d.ts`, `my_lib_bg.wasm.d.ts` | TypeScript declarations for the runtime.                                   |

`--output dist/my_lib.js` creates `dist/` and names the files from the stem `my_lib`.

### Use in HTML

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>BoxLang App</title></head>
<body>
<script type="module">
    import { greet, calculate } from './my_lib.js';

    const result = await greet("Developer");
    document.body.textContent = result;
</script>
</body>
</html>
```

### Runtime contract

The module starts loading as soon as it is imported. It exports:

* An `async` export for each top-level BoxLang function. Use `await` to collect its result.
* `ready`, a promise that resolves when the runtime and bytecode are loaded.
* `BoxLangVM`, `run_bytecode`, `initSync` and the default `init` function from the runtime.

In a browser the module also registers `window.MatchBox.modules["my_lib"]`, `window.MatchBox.ready("my_lib")`, `window.MatchBox.State(moduleName, options)`, and fires a `matchbox:ready` event on `window` with `detail.module` set to the module name.

These modules are intended for browsers. Other JavaScript hosts may need their own WebAssembly loading integration.

### Exporting functions

Functions declared at the top level of the script are exported. The exporter collects every top-level function declaration and does not look at access modifiers.

```boxlang
function greet(name) {
    return "Hello, " & name & "!"
}

function calculate(a, b) {
    return a * b
}
```

---

## Mode 2: WASI (experimental)

Use `--target wasi` for workloads outside the browser. See [WASI deployment](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html) for experimental host support.

Native Fusion supports browser builds through `--target js`; Rust code and dependencies must support that target.

---

## Mode 3: Calling functions and loading bytecode

`BoxLangVM` is exported by every `--target js` module. It runs bytecode produced by `matchbox --build`:

```js
import { ready, BoxLangVM } from './my_lib.js';

await ready;                        // runtime is initialised

const bytes = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch('./other.bxb')).arrayBuffer());

const vm = new BoxLangVM();
vm.load_bytecode(bytes);            // runs the script's top level

// call() is async: it returns a Promise
const message = await vm.call("greet", ["BoxLang"]);
console.log(message);               // Hello, BoxLang!
```

`BoxLangVM` exposes `load_bytecode(bytes)`, asynchronous `call(name, args)`, `pump()` and `vm_ptr()`.

### Compiling source strings in the browser

The packaged browser module runs bytecode. To compile source text dynamically, include `matchbox_compiler` in a custom WebAssembly runtime. This site's `playground-runtime/` is an example; see [source builds](/getting-started/building-matchbox/index.html#browser-runtime-for-source-strings).

---

## JavaScript Interop from BoxLang

When BoxLang code is running inside the browser JS target, it can access a browser bridge through the `js` global:

```boxlang
// DOM access
title = js.document.title
js.document.getElementById("output").innerText = "Updated by BoxLang"

// Browser APIs
js.alert("Hello!")
js.console.log("Logged from BoxLang")

// Location
url = js.location.href
```

The important current rule is:

* Plain JS values cross the boundary as BoxLang values: strings, booleans, null, numbers, arrays, and plain objects.
* Browser host objects stay as JS handles: DOM nodes, `document`, `window`, functions, and other browser-native objects.

That keeps state/data interop predictable while preserving access to real browser objects.
> `js.*` is a browser-only surface. Using it in a native build throws a runtime error.

---

## Serving Locally for Development

Browsers block WASM file loading over `file://`. Serve your project with any local HTTP server:

```bash
npx serve .
# or
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

Then open `http://localhost:8080` in your browser.

---

## Production Deployment

The WASM output files (`*.js` + `*.wasm`) can be deployed to any static hosting service:

* **CDN**: upload to S3, Cloudflare R2, or a similar object store.
* **Vercel / Netlify**: drop the files into your project's output directory.

Ensure your server sets the correct `Content-Type` for `.wasm` files:

    Content-Type: application/wasm

Most modern hosts handle this automatically.

title: JIT compilation
body: MatchBox includes a multi-tier JIT compiler built on Cranelift . It profiles hot code at runtime and compiles it to native machine code, eliminating interpreter dispatch overhead for the loops and functions that matter most. Where JIT is Available JIT is available in native builds with the jit feature, including the default CLI and native runners built with it. Browser/WASI and ESP32 builds use the interpreter. A browser's WebAssembly engine may optimize the module independently. The Four Tiers The JIT uses a tiered strategy: cheap profiling runs first, and compilation only fires once a site has proven itself hot. Tier 1: Empty loop elimination Trigger: A for loop whose body is empty, after ≥ 10 000 iterations. The entire loop is replaced by a single select instruction: the counter jumps straight to its final value in one native call. No iteration actually occurs. Tier 2: Numeric loop body Trigger: A for loop with a numeric-only body, after ≥ 10 000 cumulative iterations (counter persists across fiber scheduler quanta). The loop body is translated to Cranelift SSA IR. Local variables live in registers throughout; only the final values are written back to the VM's locals array on exit. Inline-cached struct member reads (monomorphic or bi-morphic) are also supported. Tier 3: Array iteration Trigger: A for-in loop over a float-only array, after ≥ 5 000 cumulative iterations. The array data pointer and length are passed directly to the compiled loop, bypassing the iterator protocol entirely. Tier 4: Hot function compilation Trigger: A function body that passes a translatability check, after ≥ 100 calls. The entire function body is compiled to a native fn(locals_ptr, heap_ptr, out_val_ptr) -> status function. Supported operations: Category Opcodes Locals GET_LOCAL , SET_LOCAL , SET_LOCAL_POP Constants Numeric literals Arithmetic ADD , SUB , MUL , DIV , MOD (float and int variants) Comparison == , != , < , <= , > , >= Boolean NOT Control flow JUMP , JUMP_IF_FALSE (forward jumps) Stack POP , DUP Calls CALL (direct calls to other JIT-compiled functions) Strings STRING_CONCAT ( & operator, via jit_concat runtime helper) Return RETURN If any unsupported opcode is present, the function is silently skipped and keeps running in the interpreter with no correctness impact. If a type guard fails at runtime (for example a variable expected to be numeric turns out to be a heap pointer), the compiled frame deopts : execution transfers back to the interpreter at the current bytecode position. Deopts are counted per function, and a function that keeps deopting is recompiled in a more tolerant mode ( crates/matchbox-vm/src/vm/jit.rs , inc_fn_deopt ): Deopts of one function Action 5 Recompile in Mode 1 (polymorphic). Arithmetic keeps its numeric fast path and falls back to a runtime helper when an operand is not a number. 10 (after Mode 1) Recompile in Mode 2 (relaxed). Arithmetic always goes through the helper. Each upgrade drops the compiled code and sets the call counter to 10 below the threshold, so the function is recompiled after 10 more calls. Mode 0 is the first compile. Each step prints a [JIT] Tier-4 function ... deopted N times. Upgrading to Mode ... line to stderr. What Is Not Supported in Tier 4 The following categories cause a function to remain interpreted: Global variables : GET_GLOBAL , SET_GLOBAL , DEFINE_GLOBAL , GET_PRIVATE , SET_PRIVATE I/O : PRINT , PRINTLN Object / collection creation : NEW , ARRAY , STRUCT Property and index access : MEMBER , SET_MEMBER , INC_MEMBER , INDEX , SET_INDEX Dynamic calls : INVOKE , INVOKE_NAMED , CALL_NAMED Loops inside functions : FOR_LOOP_STEP , LOOP , ITER_NEXT Exception handling : PUSH_HANDLER , POP_HANDLER , THROW Multi-word compare-jumps : LOCAL_COMPARE_JUMP , GLOBAL_COMPARE_JUMP , COMPARE_JUMP , LOCAL_JUMP_IF_NE_CONST Miscellaneous : INC , DEC , INC_LOCAL , INC_GLOBAL , SWAP , OVER , JUMP_IF_NULL In practice, Tier 4 is most effective for pure computational functions: numeric kernels, string-building loops, recursive math, and hot helper functions that operate only on their arguments and local variables. They are not controlled by --verbose . Opting Out To build the CLI without the JIT, leave out jit and also server . The matchbox_server crate enables jit on the VM itself, so with server on the JIT cannot be switched off ( cargo tree -e features shows cranelift-jit for any feature set that includes server ). cargo build --release --no-default-features \ --features "bif-io,bif-jni,bif-crypto,bif-cli,bif-http" This drops --serve and --target wasi-http along with the JIT. The dependency tree for this command contains no cranelift-jit and no axum ; it was inspected, not built. Future Directions JIT in native runner stubs The build.rs feature-forwarding block (the features list at lines 92 to 108) explicitly lists which features are passed to matchbox-runner stub builds. Adding "jit" there would give deployed native runner stubs the same JIT benefits as the CLI's local interpreter. The trade-off is binary size: Cranelift would be linked into every stub, which multiplies across targets in cross-compile mode. When that trade-off becomes acceptable, the change is a one-liner in build.rs : if env::var("CARGO_FEATURE_JIT").is_ok() { features.push("jit"); } Wider Tier-4 opcode coverage The most impactful missing opcodes for real-world functions are globals and property access. Both are achievable with runtime helpers following the same pattern as jit_concat and jit_ic_member_fallback . The main constraint is the deopt story: any operation that can throw or have side effects needs a clean deopt path back to the interpreter. String constant support in Tier-4 Currently, CONSTANT only accepts numeric literals in compiled functions. String constants require the GC heap at JIT-compile time, which isn't available. One path forward: a jit_intern_const helper that lazily allocates the string object on first call and caches its GC id, making string constants safe to use from compiled frames. Tier-4 for embedded loops Functions containing FOR_LOOP_STEP are currently rejected by fn_is_translatable . Supporting them would require the Tier-2 loop compiler to operate within Tier-4's SSA frame, essentially merging the two tiers. The deopt model is the main complexity: a loop inside a compiled function that deopts mid-iteration needs to restore both the function's locals and the loop counter.
markdown:
MatchBox includes a multi-tier JIT compiler built on [Cranelift](https://cranelift.dev/). It profiles hot code at runtime and compiles it to native machine code, eliminating interpreter dispatch overhead for the loops and functions that matter most.

---

## Where JIT is Available

JIT is available in native builds with the `jit` feature, including the default CLI and native runners built with it. Browser/WASI and ESP32 builds use the interpreter. A browser's WebAssembly engine may optimize the module independently.

---

## The Four Tiers

The JIT uses a tiered strategy: cheap profiling runs first, and compilation only fires once a site has proven itself hot.

### Tier 1: Empty loop elimination

**Trigger:** A `for` loop whose body is empty, after ≥ 10 000 iterations.

The entire loop is replaced by a single `select` instruction: the counter jumps straight to its final value in one native call. No iteration actually occurs.

### Tier 2: Numeric loop body

**Trigger:** A `for` loop with a numeric-only body, after ≥ 10 000 cumulative iterations (counter persists across fiber scheduler quanta).

The loop body is translated to Cranelift SSA IR. Local variables live in registers throughout; only the final values are written back to the VM's locals array on exit. Inline-cached struct member reads (monomorphic or bi-morphic) are also supported.

### Tier 3: Array iteration

**Trigger:** A `for-in` loop over a float-only array, after ≥ 5 000 cumulative iterations.

The array data pointer and length are passed directly to the compiled loop, bypassing the iterator protocol entirely.

### Tier 4: Hot function compilation

**Trigger:** A function body that passes a translatability check, after ≥ 100 calls.

The entire function body is compiled to a native `fn(locals_ptr, heap_ptr, out_val_ptr) -> status` function. Supported operations:

| Category     | Opcodes                                                         |
|:-------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Locals       | `GET_LOCAL`, `SET_LOCAL`, `SET_LOCAL_POP`                       |
| Constants    | Numeric literals                                                |
| Arithmetic   | `ADD`, `SUB`, `MUL`, `DIV`, `MOD` (float and int variants)      |
| Comparison   | `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`                                |
| Boolean      | `NOT`                                                           |
| Control flow | `JUMP`, `JUMP_IF_FALSE` (forward jumps)                         |
| Stack        | `POP`, `DUP`                                                    |
| Calls        | `CALL` (direct calls to other JIT-compiled functions)           |
| Strings      | `STRING_CONCAT` (`&` operator, via `jit_concat` runtime helper) |
| Return       | `RETURN`                                                        |

If any unsupported opcode is present, the function is silently skipped and keeps running in the interpreter with no correctness impact. If a type guard fails at runtime (for example a variable expected to be numeric turns out to be a heap pointer), the compiled frame **deopts**: execution transfers back to the interpreter at the current bytecode position.

Deopts are counted per function, and a function that keeps deopting is recompiled in a more tolerant mode (`crates/matchbox-vm/src/vm/jit.rs`, `inc_fn_deopt`):

| Deopts of one function | Action                                                                                                                                            |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 5                      | Recompile in **Mode 1** (polymorphic). Arithmetic keeps its numeric fast path and falls back to a runtime helper when an operand is not a number. |
| 10 (after Mode 1)      | Recompile in **Mode 2** (relaxed). Arithmetic always goes through the helper.                                                                     |

Each upgrade drops the compiled code and sets the call counter to 10 below the threshold, so the function is recompiled after 10 more calls. Mode 0 is the first compile. Each step prints a `[JIT] Tier-4 function ... deopted N times. Upgrading to Mode ...` line to stderr.

---

## What Is Not Supported in Tier 4

The following categories cause a function to remain interpreted:

* **Global variables** : `GET_GLOBAL`, `SET_GLOBAL`, `DEFINE_GLOBAL`, `GET_PRIVATE`, `SET_PRIVATE`
* **I/O** : `PRINT`, `PRINTLN`
* **Object / collection creation** : `NEW`, `ARRAY`, `STRUCT`
* **Property and index access** : `MEMBER`, `SET_MEMBER`, `INC_MEMBER`, `INDEX`, `SET_INDEX`
* **Dynamic calls** : `INVOKE`, `INVOKE_NAMED`, `CALL_NAMED`
* **Loops inside functions** : `FOR_LOOP_STEP`, `LOOP`, `ITER_NEXT`
* **Exception handling** : `PUSH_HANDLER`, `POP_HANDLER`, `THROW`
* **Multi-word compare-jumps** : `LOCAL_COMPARE_JUMP`, `GLOBAL_COMPARE_JUMP`, `COMPARE_JUMP`, `LOCAL_JUMP_IF_NE_CONST`
* **Miscellaneous** : `INC`, `DEC`, `INC_LOCAL`, `INC_GLOBAL`, `SWAP`, `OVER`, `JUMP_IF_NULL`

In practice, Tier 4 is most effective for pure computational functions: numeric kernels, string-building loops, recursive math, and hot helper functions that operate only on their arguments and local variables.

---

## Diagnostics

The JIT reports through `eprintln!`, so its `[JIT] ...` lines (`compiled hot fn`, `compiled empty loop`, `compiled generic loop`, `compiled iter loop`, deopt upgrades and compile failures) go to stderr, not stdout. They are not controlled by `--verbose`.

---

## Opting Out

To build the CLI without the JIT, leave out `jit` and also `server`. The `matchbox_server` crate enables `jit` on the VM itself, so with `server` on the JIT cannot be switched off (`cargo tree -e features` shows `cranelift-jit` for any feature set that includes `server`).

```bash
cargo build --release --no-default-features \
  --features "bif-io,bif-jni,bif-crypto,bif-cli,bif-http"
```

This drops `--serve` and `--target wasi-http` along with the JIT. The dependency tree for this command contains no `cranelift-jit` and no `axum`; it was inspected, not built.

---

## Future Directions

### JIT in native runner stubs

The `build.rs` feature-forwarding block (the `features` list at lines 92 to 108) explicitly lists which features are passed to `matchbox-runner` stub builds. Adding `"jit"` there would give deployed native runner stubs the same JIT benefits as the CLI's local interpreter. The trade-off is binary size: Cranelift would be linked into every stub, which multiplies across targets in cross-compile mode. When that trade-off becomes acceptable, the change is a one-liner in `build.rs`:

```rust
if env::var("CARGO_FEATURE_JIT").is_ok() { features.push("jit"); }
```

### Wider Tier-4 opcode coverage

The most impactful missing opcodes for real-world functions are globals and property access. Both are achievable with runtime helpers following the same pattern as `jit_concat` and `jit_ic_member_fallback`. The main constraint is the deopt story: any operation that can throw or have side effects needs a clean deopt path back to the interpreter.

### String constant support in Tier-4

Currently, `CONSTANT` only accepts numeric literals in compiled functions. String constants require the GC heap at JIT-compile time, which isn't available. One path forward: a `jit_intern_const` helper that lazily allocates the string object on first call and caches its GC id, making string constants safe to use from compiled frames.

### Tier-4 for embedded loops

Functions containing `FOR_LOOP_STEP` are currently rejected by `fn_is_translatable`. Supporting them would require the Tier-2 loop compiler to operate within Tier-4's SSA frame, essentially merging the two tiers. The deopt model is the main complexity: a loop inside a compiled function that deopts mid-iteration needs to restore both the function's locals and the loop counter.

| [Modules](/reference/language/modules/index.html)                                              | `--module`, `ModuleConfig.bx`, discovery                                           |
| [Java interop](/reference/language/java-interop/index.html)                                    | The JNI bridge and its limits                                                      |
| [Queries and data](/reference/language/query-and-data/index.html)                              | `queryNew`, datasources, query of queries, build features                          |

## File types

| Extension |                                       Use                                       |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `.bxs`    | Script. Run with `matchbox file.bxs`.                                           |
| `.bx`     | Class file, resolved by `new` and `import`. Also accepted as a module BIF file. |
| `.bxm`    | Template. Run with `matchbox file.bxm` or serve with `--serve`.                 |
| `.bxb`    | Compiled bytecode, produced by `matchbox --build`.                              |

`.cfm`, `.cfc` and `.cfs` files are not supported. `matchbox page.cfm` fails with a parse error.

For an overview of runtime and target differences, see [BoxLang compatibility](/differences-from-boxlang/index.html).

title: Learn MatchBox
body: MatchBox is the Rust runtime for BoxLang. This course takes you from a first script to a native executable in ten short lessons. You do not need to install anything to start: every code sample has a Run this in your browser button that opens a real MatchBox runtime, compiled to WebAssembly, right under the code. Edit the sample, break it, run it again. Your progress is remembered in this browser, so you can stop and pick up where you left off. Continue where you left off: Welcome to MatchBox What MatchBox is, how it relates to BoxLang, and your first script, run in the browser. Install and run Install MatchBox with MVM, then run and compile a script on your own machine. Values and strings Variables, numbers, strings, interpolation and operators. Arrays and structs Lists and key-value data, and the loops that walk over them. Functions and callbacks Functions, default and named arguments, arrow functions, and map, filter and reduce. Classes and objects Bundle data and behavior together, with a constructor and methods you can chain. Errors and control flow if and switch, break and continue, and handling errors with try, catch and finally. Running work at the same time Futures, runAsync and then, and how the browser build runs them. Build and ship Turn a script into bytecode or a single native executable you can hand to anyone. Where to go next Choose your next project and explore the tools for your deployment target. Before you start You should know the basics of at least one programming language. You do not need to know BoxLang, CFML or Rust. The lessons that install tools or build files (lessons 2 and 9) show commands for your own terminal, because a browser tab cannot do those. Everything else runs on this page. The playground has limits: a run stops after 5 seconds, source and output are capped at 64 KiB, and there are no files, network or Java. title: Modules
body: A module is a reusable BoxLang package. It can provide functions, classes, components and settings, with an optional native backend for MatchBox. Using a module Install a MatchBox-compatible package in boxlang_modules/ , or select its directory explicitly: matchbox --module ./libs/greeter app.bxs Project modules take precedence over shared packages in BOXLANG_HOME/modules/ . Package dependencies and explicit paths can also be declared in project configuration . Package layout greeter/ box.json ModuleConfig.bx bifs/ models/ components/ ModuleConfig.bx defines the module's settings and lifecycle: class { function configure() { settings = { greeting: "Hello" }; } function onLoad() {} function onUnload() {} } At runtime, MatchBox configures modules and loads their dependencies before calling onLoad() . onUnload() handles cleanup during normal shutdown. Application settings can override module defaults. Read a module's settings with: println( getModuleSettings( "greeter" ).greeting ); Native functionality Compatible modules can ship prebuilt native plugins, so consumers do not need a Rust toolchain. The plugin must match the destination platform; native code runs with the application's permissions. For application-owned Rust code, use Native Fusion . Modules that depend on JVM libraries need a compatible MatchBox backend rather than assuming those libraries are present. For plugin authoring details, see the MatchBox repository's native module guide .
markdown:
A module is a reusable BoxLang package. It can provide functions, classes, components and settings, with an optional native backend for MatchBox.

## Using a module

Install a MatchBox-compatible package in `boxlang_modules/`, or select its directory explicitly:

```sh
matchbox --module ./libs/greeter app.bxs
```

Project modules take precedence over shared packages in `BOXLANG_HOME/modules/`. Package dependencies and explicit paths can also be declared in [project configuration](/reference/configuration/index.html).

## Package layout

```text
greeter/
  box.json
  ModuleConfig.bx
  bifs/
  models/
  components/
```

`ModuleConfig.bx` defines the module's settings and lifecycle:

```boxlang
class {
    function configure() {
        settings = { greeting: "Hello" };
    }

    function onLoad() {}
    function onUnload() {}
}
```

At runtime, MatchBox configures modules and loads their dependencies before calling `onLoad()`. `onUnload()` handles cleanup during normal shutdown. Application settings can override module defaults.

Read a module's settings with:

```boxlang
println( getModuleSettings( "greeter" ).greeting );
```

## Native functionality

Compatible modules can ship prebuilt native plugins, so consumers do not need a Rust toolchain. The plugin must match the destination platform; native code runs with the application's permissions.

For application-owned Rust code, use [Native Fusion](/building-and-deploying/native-fusion/index.html). Modules that depend on JVM libraries need a compatible MatchBox backend rather than assuming those libraries are present.

For plugin authoring details, see the MatchBox repository's [native module guide](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox/blob/develop/docs/native-plugins.md).

title: Native Builds
body: Build a standalone executable with the MatchBox runner and your compiled BoxLang code. The destination does not need a separate MatchBox installation or Java for ordinary BoxLang execution. Build for the current host matchbox --target native my_app.bxs ./my_app On Windows, run my_app.exe . Use --output <path> before the source file to choose a different output name. Package from .bxs or .bxm source. A .bxb file is already compiled bytecode and is run directly, not repackaged by --target native . What is in the executable MatchBox combines a prebuilt runner, called a stub, with the application's bytecode. BoxLang still runs on the VM; it is not translated into machine code by this packaging step. Binary size depends on the runner, enabled features and application. Host integrations and native modules can add dependencies of their own. Running a native executable Pass script arguments directly to the executable: ./my_app first second --name=bob Read them with cliGetArgs() . Use cliExit(n) to set an exit code; an unhandled runtime error exits with a failure status. Build for other hosts Choose a Rust target triple when the CLI includes a runner for that platform: matchbox --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu my_app.bxs Release CLIs include cross-platform runners. Custom source builds can use the cross-compile feature; available runners depend on the build toolchains. See Building MatchBox . Test the artifact on its destination operating system and architecture. Native libraries must match that platform too. Rust interoperability Native Fusion compiles Rust code into the application alongside BoxLang. It needs Rust, the MatchBox source checkout and the toolchain for the destination target.
markdown:
Build a standalone executable with the MatchBox runner and your compiled BoxLang code. The destination does not need a separate MatchBox installation or Java for ordinary BoxLang execution.

## Build for the current host

```sh
matchbox --target native my_app.bxs
./my_app
```

On Windows, run `my_app.exe`. Use `--output <path>` before the source file to choose a different output name.

Package from `.bxs` or `.bxm` source. A `.bxb` file is already compiled bytecode and is run directly, not repackaged by `--target native`.

## What is in the executable

MatchBox combines a prebuilt runner, called a stub, with the application's bytecode. BoxLang still runs on the VM; it is not translated into machine code by this packaging step.

Binary size depends on the runner, enabled features and application. Host integrations and native modules can add dependencies of their own.

## Running a native executable

Pass script arguments directly to the executable:

```sh
./my_app first second --name=bob
```

Read them with `cliGetArgs()`. Use `cliExit(n)` to set an exit code; an unhandled runtime error exits with a failure status.

## Build for other hosts

Choose a Rust target triple when the CLI includes a runner for that platform:

```sh
matchbox --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu my_app.bxs
```

Release CLIs include cross-platform runners. Custom source builds can use the `cross-compile` feature; available runners depend on the build toolchains. See [Building MatchBox](/getting-started/building-matchbox/index.html).

Test the artifact on its destination operating system and architecture. Native libraries must match that platform too.

## Rust interoperability

[Native Fusion](/building-and-deploying/native-fusion/index.html) compiles Rust code into the application alongside BoxLang. It needs Rust, the MatchBox source checkout and the toolchain for the destination target.

title: Native Fusion example
body: Native Fusion lets you write performance-critical functions and stateful objects in Rust and use them directly from BoxLang. Everything is statically linked into a single native binary - no external libraries, no FFI boilerplate at call sites. This example demonstrates both interop styles: Style Rust side BoxLang side Standalone BIF #[matchbox_fn] on a plain function result = fast_fib(10) Native object #[matchbox_class] + #[matchbox_methods] on a struct s = new rust:stats.RunningStats() Project Layout native_fusion/ ├── app.bxs ← BoxLang entry point └── native/ └── stats.rs ← Rust source: BIFs + RunningStats native object MatchBox automatically detects any .rs files inside a native/ directory that lives alongside your entry script and compiles them together with the VM. Building You need a Rust toolchain ( cargo , rustc ) in addition to the matchbox binary. The generated Cargo project depends on the crates/matchbox-vm directory of the MatchBox source tree that built your matchbox binary, so that tree must still exist on disk at its original path. The first build compiles the VM and takes a minute or more. cd docs/examples/native_fusion matchbox --target native app.bxs MatchBox will: Compile native/stats.rs together with the MatchBox VM. Register the exported BIFs ( fast_fib , fast_factorial ) and the RunningStats class. Compile app.bxs to bytecode and embed it. Produce a single app binary. Running ./app Expected output: === Native Fusion Demo === --- Fibonacci (BIF) --- fib(0) = 0 fib(1) = 1 fib(2) = 1 ... fib(10) = 55 --- Factorials (BIF) --- 1! = 1 2! = 2 ... 10! = 3628800 --- RunningStats (native object) --- count : 6 sum : 108 mean : 18 min : 4 max : 42 All results computed in Rust. Writing a Native BIF with #[matchbox_fn] Using the #[matchbox_fn] macro is the recommended way to write BIFs. You write a plain typed Rust function - the macro generates the {name}_wrapper with the correct BIF signature, argument-count validation, and type coercions for you. use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn}; // Write a normal Rust function with typed parameters. // Supported types: f64, i32, bool, String, BxValue (pass-through) #[matchbox_fn] pub fn my_bif(n: f64) -> f64 { n * 2.0 } The macro expands this into two things: Your original my_bif(n: f64) -> f64 function, unchanged. A generated my_bif_wrapper(vm, args) -> Result<BxValue, String> that the VM actually calls. Each .rs file inside native/ must export a register_bifs() function. Register the _wrapper variant (not the original function): use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn, types::{BxNativeFunction, BxValue}}; use std::collections::HashMap; #[matchbox_fn] pub fn my_bif(n: f64) -> f64 { n * 2.0 } pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Register the macro-generated wrapper, not the plain function. map.insert("my_bif".to_string(), my_bif_wrapper as BxNativeFunction); map } The string key ( "my_bif" ) is the name BoxLang uses to call the function: result = my_bif(21) println(result) // 42 Supported Parameter Types Rust type Macro conversion f64 args[i].as_number() i32 args[i].as_int() bool args[i].as_bool() String vm.to_string(args[i]) BxValue passed through as-is Native Objects with #[matchbox_class] and #[matchbox_methods] For stateful interop, expose a Rust struct as a BoxLang native object. use matchbox_vm::{ matchbox_class, matchbox_methods, types::{BxNativeFunction, BxNativeObject, BxValue, BxVM}, }; use std::cell::RefCell; use std::collections::HashMap; use std::rc::Rc; // #[matchbox_class] auto-implements the BxNativeObject trait, // wiring get_property / set_property / call_method to the // dispatcher generated by #[matchbox_methods]. #[matchbox_class] #[derive(Debug)] pub struct Counter { pub value: f64, } // #[matchbox_methods] generates a dispatch_method() router that maps // BoxLang method names (case-insensitive) to the Rust methods below. #[matchbox_methods] impl Counter { pub fn increment(&mut self) -> f64 { self.value += 1.0; self.value } pub fn add(&mut self, n: f64) -> f64 { self.value += n; self.value } pub fn get(&self) -> f64 { self.value } } // Constructor - called when BoxLang evaluates `new rust:mymodule.Counter(0)`. // vm.native_object_new() stores the object on the VM heap and returns an id // wrapped in a BxValue pointer. pub fn create_counter(vm: &mut dyn BxVM, args: &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> { let initial = args.first().map(|v| v.as_number()).unwrap_or(0.0); let obj = Counter { value: initial }; let id = vm.native_object_new(Rc::new(RefCell::new(obj))); Ok(BxValue::new_ptr(id)) } // register_classes() maps "<module>.<ClassName>" to the constructor. // The module name is the filename of this .rs file without the extension. // BoxLang resolves `new rust:mymodule.Counter()` using this key. pub fn register_classes() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("mymodule.Counter".to_string(), create_counter as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang: c = new rust:mymodule.Counter(0) c.increment() c.add(9) println(c.get()) // 10 When to Use Native Fusion You need maximum throughput on a hot path (parsing, compression, crypto, ML). You want to use a Rust crate ( serde , image , reqwest , etc.) from BoxLang. You need direct OS or hardware access. For most application logic, plain BoxLang is sufficient. Reserve Native Fusion for the innermost loops where performance is measured and critical. Limitations Feature Status Supported targets Native, browser/JavaScript, WASI (experimental), and ESP32; Rust code must support the target. Multiple .rs files in native/ ✅ Each may export register_bifs() and/or register_classes() Using external Rust crates Add a Cargo.toml to native/ . Mutable self in #[matchbox_methods] ✅ Dispatcher takes &mut self Property access on native objects ⚠️ Override get_property in BxNativeObject manually For the full macro API reference see native-fusion.md .

title: Native Fusion reference
body: Native Fusion links Rust functions and objects into your BoxLang application. It supports every MatchBox target: native, browser/JavaScript, WASI and ESP32. Rust code and dependencies must support the selected target. Browser builds cannot use desktop OS APIs, and ESP32 code must fit the device. WASI remains experimental . How It Works Create a native/ directory alongside your .bxs entry script. Write one or more .rs files inside native/ . Each .rs file exports a register_bifs() and/or register_classes() function. Run matchbox --target native app.bxs . Native Fusion detected! Target: native. Building hybrid artifact... ... Native Fusion binary produced: app MatchBox detects native/ , generates a temporary Cargo project that contains the .rs files, the bytecode and the VM, merges all BIF and class registrations, builds it with Cargo for the selected target, and writes the artifact. You need Rust, the target's toolchain and the MatchBox source checkout used to build the CLI. Builds may run offline; cache dependencies first. Macros All interop macros are re-exported from the matchbox_vm crate, so no separate matchbox_macros import is needed: use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn, matchbox_class, matchbox_methods}; #[matchbox_fn] : Expose a Rust function as a BoxLang BIF Annotate a plain Rust function with typed parameters. The macro generates a corresponding {name}_wrapper function that carries the low-level BIF signature expected by the VM ( fn(&mut dyn BxVM, &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> ). The wrapper handles argument-count validation and type coercion automatically. Usage use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn, types::{BxNativeFunction}}; use std::collections::HashMap; #[matchbox_fn] pub fn add(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 { a + b } pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Register the generated wrapper, not the original function. map.insert("add".to_string(), add_wrapper as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang: result = add(10, 20) println(result) // 30 Supported Parameter Types Rust parameter type VM conversion applied by the macro f64 args[i].as_number() i32 args[i].as_int() bool args[i].as_bool() String vm.to_string(args[i]) BxValue passed through unchanged The return value is always wrapped as BxValue::new_number(result as f64) . For BIFs that need to return other types (strings, null, objects), write a manual BIF instead (see Manual BIF Signature ). What the Macro Generates // Your function: unchanged: pub fn add(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 { a + b } // Generated wrapper: pub fn add_wrapper( vm: &mut dyn matchbox_vm::types::BxVM, args: &[matchbox_vm::types::BxValue], ) -> Result<matchbox_vm::types::BxValue, String> { if args.len() != 2 { return Err(format!("add requires 2 arguments, got {}", args.len())); } let a = args[0].as_number(); let b = args[1].as_number(); let result = add(a, b); Ok(matchbox_vm::types::BxValue::new_number(result as f64)) } #[matchbox_class] : Expose a Rust struct as a BoxLang native object Annotate a struct to auto-implement the BxNativeObject trait. The generated implementation delegates get_property , set_property , and call_method to a dispatch_method function that is generated by #[matchbox_methods] . Always pair #[matchbox_class] with a #[matchbox_methods] impl block. Usage use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_class, matchbox_methods, types::{BxValue, BxVM, BxNativeFunction, BxNativeObject}}; use std::collections::HashMap; use std::rc::Rc; use std::cell::RefCell; #[matchbox_class] #[derive(Debug)] pub struct Counter { pub value: f64, } #[matchbox_methods] impl Counter { pub fn increment(&mut self) -> f64 { self.value += 1.0; self.value } pub fn add(&mut self, n: f64) -> f64 { self.value += n; self.value } pub fn get(&self) -> f64 { self.value } } // Constructor: registered separately, not via #[matchbox_fn]. pub fn create_counter(vm: &mut dyn BxVM, args: &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> { let initial = args.first().map(|v| v.as_number()).unwrap_or(0.0); let obj = Counter { value: initial }; let id = vm.native_object_new(Rc::new(RefCell::new(obj))); Ok(BxValue::new_ptr(id)) } pub fn register_classes() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Key format: "<module_filename>.<ClassName>" // This file is native/counter.rs → module name is "counter" map.insert("counter.Counter".to_string(), create_counter as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang (instantiate with new rust:<module>.<Class>(...) ): c = new rust:counter.Counter(0) c.increment() c.add(9) println(c.get()) // 10 #[matchbox_methods] : Generate a method dispatcher for a native class Annotate an impl block to generate a dispatch_method function that routes BoxLang method calls to the correct Rust method by name (case-insensitive). #[matchbox_fn] type-coercion rules apply to each method's parameters. Usage #[matchbox_methods] impl MyStruct { pub fn process(&self, input: f64) -> f64 { input * self.factor } } BoxLang calls obj.process(42) and the dispatcher resolves it to MyStruct::process(&self, 42.0) . What the Macro Generates impl MyStruct { fn dispatch_method( &mut self, vm: &mut dyn BxVM, name: &str, args: &[BxValue], ) -> Result<BxValue, String> { match name.to_lowercase().as_str() { "process" => { if args.len() != 1 { return Err(...); } let input = args[0].as_number(); let result = self.process(input); Ok(BxValue::new_number(result as f64)) } _ => Err(format!("Method {} not found", name)), } } } #[matchbox_module] : Module marker (no-op) A no-op attribute that serves as documentation: apply it to the top-level mod or impl to indicate the file is a Native Fusion module. Currently passes through unchanged. #[matchbox_module] mod my_native_module { ... } Registration Entry Points Every .rs file in native/ may export two entry-point functions. MatchBox calls them both at startup. register_bifs() : standalone functions pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("my_bif".to_string(), my_bif_wrapper as BxNativeFunction); map } BIF names must be unique across all files in native/ . register_classes() : native object constructors pub fn register_classes() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Key: "<module>.<ClassName>" where <module> is the filename without .rs map.insert("mymodule.MyClass".to_string(), create_my_class as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang uses the key to resolve new rust:mymodule.MyClass(...) . Manual BIF Signature When you need full control (e.g. returning a string, null, or an object pointer), skip #[matchbox_fn] and write the low-level signature directly: use matchbox_vm::types::{BxNativeFunction, BxValue, BxVM}; use std::collections::HashMap; pub fn greet(vm: &mut dyn BxVM, args: &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> { if args.is_empty() { return Err("greet: expected one argument".to_string()); } let name = vm.to_string(args[0]); Ok(BxValue::new_ptr(vm.string_new(format!("Hello, {}!", name)))) } pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("greet".to_string(), greet as BxNativeFunction); map } Project Layout my_app/ ├── app.bxs ← BoxLang entry point └── native/ ├── math.rs ← exports register_bifs() ├── counter.rs ← exports register_bifs() + register_classes() └── crypto.rs ← exports register_classes() Multiple files are supported as long as BIF and class names are unique across all files. Using External Rust Crates Declare dependencies in native/Cargo.toml : [dependencies] semver = "1" MatchBox merges them into the generated build. Relative path dependencies resolve against native/ . Do not redeclare crates supplied by Fusion, such as matchbox_vm . Reusable native functionality can also live in a module . Limitations All targets support Fusion, but Rust APIs and dependencies must match the target. Use --target js for browsers and --target wasi for WASI hosts. Return types other than f64 from #[matchbox_fn] need a manual BIF. Native object property access requires get_property in BxNativeObject . See native-builds.md for the complete native build reference and differences-from-boxlang.md for the full list of features not available in MatchBox.

#[matchbox_class] : Expose a Rust struct as a BoxLang native object
#[matchbox_methods] : Generate a method dispatcher for a native class

title: Operators
body: BoxLang provides symbolic and word operators for calculations, comparisons and control flow. Arithmetic and strings Operator Meaning Example Result + - * / Arithmetic 10 / 4 2.5 % , mod Remainder, sign follows the left operand -7 % 3 -1 \ Integer division 10 \ 3 3 ^ Power 2 ^ 10 1024 & String concatenation "abc" & 1 abc1 += -= *= /= %= &= Compound assignment x = 10; x %= 3 1 ++ -- Increment and decrement i++ Use + for arithmetic and & for joining text. Numeric strings can participate in arithmetic: "5" + "6" is 11 . Division by zero throws an error. Comparison and logic println( 5 == 5 ); println( 5 eq 5 ); println( 5 neq 4 ); println( 5 != 4 ); println( 3 lte 3 ); println( 3 gte 4 ); println( "a" < "b" ); println( 1 is 1 ); println( "abc" contains "B" ); println( "abc" does not contain "x" ); println( true && false || true ); println( true and false ); println( true xor false ); println( 1 eqv 1 ); println( !false ); Output: true true true true true false true true true true true false true true true String comparison ignores case: "a" == "A" is true . === behaves like == , which BoxLang does too. Use ! or not for negation, && or and for conjunction, and || or or for alternatives. Bitwise BoxLang spells bitwise operators with a b prefix. println( 5 b& 3 ); println( 5 b| 3 ); println( 5 b^ 3 ); println( b~ 5 ); println( 1 b<< 4 ); println( 256 b>> 4 ); println( 16 b>>> 2 ); Output: 1 7 6 -6 16 16 4 Both operands must be numbers. castAs and instanceOf castAs takes the type name as a string. Wrap it in parentheses when you combine it with other operators, because the string after castAs swallows what follows. println( ( 5 castAs "string" ) & "!" ); println( ( "3.5" castAs "numeric" ) + 1 ); println( "yes" castAs "boolean" ); println( "a" instanceOf "string" ); println( 1 instanceOf "numeric" ); println( { } instanceOf "struct" ); println( [ ] instanceOf "array" ); println( ( x => x ) instanceOf "function" ); println( 1 instanceOf "string" ); Output: 5! 4.5 true true true true true true false "abc" castAs "numeric" throws BoxCastException: Could not cast object [abc] to type [numeric] . 7.9 castAs "integer" throws a BoxCastException . BoxLang does too. x castAs string without quotes fails. setValue instanceOf "set" is false for a set . Elvis, ternary and safe navigation n = null; println( n ?: "was null" ); println( "" ?: "not used" ); println( 5 > 3 ? "yes" : "no" ); s = { a: { b: 2 } }; println( s?.a?.b ); println( s.missing?.deeper ?: "safe" ); println( isNull( n?.a ) ); Output: was null yes 2 safe true ?: only replaces null. An empty string passes through, so the second line prints an empty line. A ?. guards only the step it is on. n?.a.b with n null throws Member access only supported on structs, instances, JS objects, and native objects . BoxLang returns null. Write n?.a?.b . For sets and ranges see sets and destructuring, spread and ranges .

title: Queries and data
body: A query is a table of rows and named columns. You can build one in memory or obtain one from a database. Database functions are available in native builds with datasource support, not in the browser playground. In-memory queries people = queryNew( "id,name", "integer,varchar", [ [ 1, "Ann" ], [ 2, "Bob" ] ] ); println( people.recordCount ); println( people.name[ 2 ] ); for ( person in people ) { println( person.id & ":" & person.name ); } 2 Bob 1:Ann 2:Bob Functions such as queryAddRow , queryGetCell , querySetCell and queryColumnData let you work with rows and columns directly. Query indexes start at 1. Datasources Register a datasource, then pass its name to queryExecute . MatchBox provides SQLite and PostgreSQL drivers. datasourceRegister( "main", { driver: "sqlite", database: "app.db" } ); people = queryExecute( "select id, name from people where id = ?", [ 1 ], { datasource: "main" } ); The example assumes the database has a people table. Use query parameters rather than joining user input into SQL. Datasources can also be declared in matchbox.toml . Transactions and query of queries Use transactionBegin , transactionCommit and transactionRollback to group database changes. Query of queries runs SQL over in-memory query data using dbtype: "query" ; it requires a build with the qoq feature. See source builds for custom runtime features and the query function reference for available functions.

title: Running work at the same time
body: A future stands for a value that is not ready yet. runAsync starts some work and hands you a future straight away. You call get() on it when you need the result. Your first future answer = runAsync( () => 6 * 7 ); println( "started" ); println( answer.get() ); Output: started 42 Several at once Start more than one future, then collect the results. slow = runAsync( () => { sleep( 20 ); return "slow"; } ); fast = runAsync( () => "fast" ); println( fast.get() & " then " & slow.get() ); Output: fast then slow Chaining then runs a function on the result when it arrives, and gives you a new future. result = runAsync( () => 10 ).then( n => n * 2 ); println( result.get() ); Output: 20 Measuring time getTickCount() returns milliseconds, and sleep( ms ) pauses. start = getTickCount(); sleep( 30 ); elapsed = getTickCount() - start; println( elapsed >= 30 ); Output: true In the browser BoxLang futures take turns on the VM's thread, in both native and browser builds. Native I/O can run independently; CPU-heavy callbacks do not run across multiple cores. The playground stops runs after five seconds. Try it Start three futures that each sleep for a different time and return a different word. Print them in the order you started them.

title: Scopes
body: A scope is a named place to store variables. Scripts, functions, classes and web requests each provide context for the values you use. Scripts and functions At script level, bare names and variables refer to script variables. Inside functions, use var or local for local values and arguments for parameters. function greet( name, greeting = "Hello" ) { var message = greeting & ", " & arguments.name; return message; } println( greet( "Ann" ) ); println( greet( greeting = "Hi", name = "Bob" ) ); Hello, Ann Hi, Bob Closures A closure can use values from its enclosing function: function adder( amount ) { return value => value + amount; } addFive = adder( 5 ); println( addFive( 10 ) ); 15 Classes Inside a class, this holds public state and variables holds private instance state. See classes . Web scopes When serving templates, MatchBox provides scopes for the current request: Scope Contents url Query-string parameters. form Posted form fields. cookie Request cookies. session State associated with the session cookie. cgi Request information such as the method and path. Web scopes belong to the server environment, not an ordinary CLI script. Session storage and application lifecycle depend on the server you use; see Web server .
markdown:
A scope is a named place to store variables. Scripts, functions, classes and web requests each provide context for the values you use.

## Scripts and functions

At script level, bare names and `variables` refer to script variables. Inside functions, use `var` or `local` for local values and `arguments` for parameters.

```boxlang
function greet( name, greeting = "Hello" ) {
    var message = greeting & ", " & arguments.name;
    return message;
}

println( greet( "Ann" ) );
println( greet( greeting = "Hi", name = "Bob" ) );
```

```text
Hello, Ann
Hi, Bob
```

## Closures

A closure can use values from its enclosing function:

```boxlang
function adder( amount ) {
    return value => value + amount;
}

addFive = adder( 5 );
println( addFive( 10 ) );
```

```text
15
```

## Classes

Inside a class, `this` holds public state and `variables` holds private instance state. See [classes](/reference/language/classes/index.html).

## Web scopes

When serving templates, MatchBox provides scopes for the current request:

|   Scope   |                     Contents                     |
|-----------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `url`     | Query-string parameters.                         |
| `form`    | Posted form fields.                              |
| `cookie`  | Request cookies.                                 |
| `session` | State associated with the session cookie.        |
| `cgi`     | Request information such as the method and path. |

Web scopes belong to the server environment, not an ordinary CLI script. Session storage and application lifecycle depend on the server you use; see [Web server](/building-and-deploying/web-server/index.html).

title: Sets
body: A set holds each value once. Create one with a literal, setNew() , setOf() or toSet() . Creating a set a = set{ 3, 1, 2, 3 }; println( a.size() ); empty = set{}; println( empty.isEmpty() ); b = setOf( "x", "y", "x" ); println( b.toList( "," ) ); c = [ 5, 5, 6 ].toSet(); println( c.toList( "," ) ); d = setNew( type = "linked", values = [ 3, 1, 2, 3 ] ); println( d.toList( "," ) ); Output: 3 true x,y 5,6 3,1,2 set{} is a literal: the word set followed by braces. setNew() takes type ( default , linked or sorted ) and values . listToSet( "a,b,a" ) and structKeySet( struct ) also return sets. Order Type Ordering default and linked Insertion order. sorted Sorted once, when setNew() builds it from values . Values you add() later are appended, not sorted. s = setNew( type = "sorted", values = [ 10, 9, 100 ] ); println( s.toList( "," ) ); s.add( 1 ); println( s.toList( "," ) ); Output: 9,10,100 9,10,100,1 A set is stored as an array that skips duplicates when it is built. isArray( s ) is true , s[ 1 ] reads the first value, println( s ) prints it like an array and serializeJSON( s ) returns an array. s instanceOf "set" is false . Operators and algebra When either operand is a set, + , - , * and ^ do set algebra, and the other operand can be an array. Operator Member function Result a + b a.union( b ) Values in either set. a - b a.difference( b ) Values in a and not in b . a * b a.intersection( b ) Values in both. a ^ b a.symmetricDifference( b ) Values in exactly one. a = setOf( 1, 2, 3 ); b = setOf( 2, 3, 4 ); println( ( a + b ).toList( "," ) ); println( ( a - b ).toList( "," ) ); println( ( a * b ).toList( "," ) ); println( ( a ^ b ).toList( "," ) ); println( a.isSubsetOf( setOf( 1, 2, 3, 4 ) ) ); println( a.isSupersetOf( setOf( 1 ) ) ); println( a.isDisjointFrom( setOf( 9 ) ) ); println( ( a + [ 3, 7 ] ).toList( "," ) ); Output: 1,2,3,4 1 2,3 1,4 true true true 1,2,3,7 Only an array works as the loose right operand. a + "7,8" is string concatenation and gives [1,2]7,8 , and [ 9 ] + a is an array join. Member functions Group Works Add and remove add , append , addAll , remove , delete , removeAll , retainAll , clear Query contains , has , size , len , length , count , isEmpty , isSubsetOf , isSupersetOf , isDisjointFrom , isCaseSensitive , isSynchronized Algebra union , intersection , difference , symmetricDifference Functional each , map , filter , reduce , every , some , none , find , reject Convert toArray , toList( delimiter ) s = setOf( 1, 2, 3, 4 ); println( s.map( x => x * 10 ).toList( "," ) ); println( s.filter( x => x > 2 ).toList( "," ) ); println( s.reduce( ( total, x ) => total + x, 0 ) ); println( s.every( x => x > 0 ) ); println( s.some( x => x > 3 ) ); println( s.none( x => x > 9 ) ); println( s.find( x => x > 2 ) ); Output: 10,20,30,40 3,4 10 true true true 3 Adding unique values Use union or + when adding values that may already exist. These operations preserve uniqueness; direct append-style methods can introduce duplicates. See also destructuring, spread and ranges and operators .

title: Single-file AWS Lambda
body: This example is the smallest MatchBox Lambda shape: Lambda.bx event.json Lambda.bx defines a class with: function run(event, context, response) The runtime passes the raw AWS Lambda event into event , an AWS-style context object into context , and a mutable Lambda proxy response struct into response . The handler here sets its own headers struct, which includes CORS headers, so the runtime's default headers are not added. The AWS Lambda guide describes the full contract, class routing and the Application.bx hooks. Local Invoke From this directory: matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json event.json is a Function URL style event with name=Lambda in the query string. The response: { "body": "{\"message\":\"Hello from Lambda\",\"path\":\"/\",\"requestId\":\"local-request\"}", "cookies": [], "headers": { "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type, Authorization", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS", "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, "isBase64Encoded": false, "statusCode": 200 } A local invoke reports local-request as the request id. AWS Setup Before deploying, follow the AWS account setup . You need: AWS CLI v2 a configured AWS profile a region an existing Lambda execution role ARN Build the bootstrap The Lambda runtime executable is not part of the CLI. Build it from the MatchBox source tree for the architecture of your function (the default is arm64 ): cargo build --release -p matchbox_lambda_runner --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu The result is target/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/matchbox_lambda_runner . Building for another architecture needs that target installed and a linker for it. Deploy matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \ --function matchbox-single-file-demo \ --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 \ --public \ --bootstrap /path/to/matchbox_lambda_runner Use --public for an unauthenticated Function URL that anyone can invoke. Use --url instead for IAM-authenticated access. Use --arch x86_64 if the bootstrap is an x86_64 build. --memory , --timeout and --out are described in the guide. If deploy succeeds, the command prints the Function URL. Test it with: curl "https://your-url.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/?name=AWS" The body has this shape: { "message": "Hello from AWS", "requestId": "...", "path": "/" }
markdown:
This example is the smallest MatchBox Lambda shape:

```text
Lambda.bx
event.json
```

`Lambda.bx` defines a class with:

```boxlang
function run(event, context, response)
```

The runtime passes the raw AWS Lambda event into `event`, an AWS-style context object into `context`, and a mutable Lambda proxy response struct into `response`. The handler here sets its own `headers` struct, which includes CORS headers, so the runtime's default headers are not added. The [AWS Lambda guide](/building-and-deploying/aws-lambda-aws-cli-setup/index.html) describes the full contract, class routing and the `Application.bx` hooks.

## Local Invoke

From this directory:

```bash
matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json
```

`event.json` is a Function URL style event with `name=Lambda` in the query string. The response:

```json
{
  "body": "{\"message\":\"Hello from Lambda\",\"path\":\"/\",\"requestId\":\"local-request\"}",
  "cookies": [],
  "headers": {
    "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type, Authorization",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "isBase64Encoded": false,
  "statusCode": 200
}
```

A local invoke reports `local-request` as the request id.

## AWS Setup

Before deploying, follow the [AWS account setup](/building-and-deploying/aws-lambda-aws-cli-setup/index.html#aws-account-setup). You need:

* AWS CLI v2
* a configured AWS profile
* a region
* an existing Lambda execution role ARN

## Build the bootstrap

The Lambda runtime executable is not part of the CLI. Build it from the MatchBox source tree for the architecture of your function (the default is `arm64`):

```bash
cargo build --release -p matchbox_lambda_runner --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

The result is `target/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/matchbox_lambda_runner`. Building for another architecture needs that target installed and a linker for it.

## Deploy

```bash
matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \
  --function matchbox-single-file-demo \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \
  --profile matchbox-dev \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --public \
  --bootstrap /path/to/matchbox_lambda_runner
```

Use `--public` for an unauthenticated Function URL that anyone can invoke. Use `--url` instead for IAM-authenticated access. Use `--arch x86_64` if the bootstrap is an x86_64 build. `--memory`, `--timeout` and `--out` are described in the guide.

If deploy succeeds, the command prints the Function URL. Test it with:

```bash
curl "https://your-url.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/?name=AWS"
```

The body has this shape:

```json
{
```

title: Values and strings
body: Variables You create a variable by assigning to it. There is no declaration keyword, and a variable can hold any type. name = "Ada"; age = 36; isAdmin = true; println( name ); println( age + 1 ); println( isAdmin ); Output: Ada 37 true Strings and interpolation Put #expression# inside a double-quoted string to insert a value. The expression can be any code. Use & to join strings. name = "Ada"; age = 36; println( "#name# is #age# years old" ); println( "Next year: #age + 1#" ); println( "Hello, " & name & "!" ); Output: Ada is 36 years old Next year: 37 Hello, Ada! To print a literal # , double it: "Issue ##42" prints Issue #42 . String functions Most string functions work both ways: ucase( text ) or text.ucase() . title = " MatchBox "; println( title.trim() ); println( title.trim().ucase() ); println( title.trim().lcase() ); println( title.trim().len() ); println( title.trim().left( 5 ) ); println( title.trim().reverse() ); println( "hello world".replace( "world", "MatchBox" ) ); println( ucFirst( "hello" ) ); Output: MatchBox MATCHBOX matchbox 8 Match xoBhctaM hello MatchBox Hello Numbers and operators println( 10 / 4 ); println( 10 \ 4 ); println( 10 % 4 ); println( 2 ^ 10 ); println( 3 > 2 ); println( true && !false ); println( 3 > 2 ? "yes" : "no" ); println( "5" + 5 ); Output: 2.5 2 2 1024 true true yes 10 / is normal division, \ divides and drops the remainder, % is the remainder and ^ is a power. Notice that "5" + 5 is 10 : BoxLang converts a numeric string to a number for arithmetic, while & always joins text. Missing values null means "no value". The elvis operator ?: supplies a default when the left side is null. nickname = null; println( nickname ?: "no nickname" ); println( isNull( nickname ) ); Output: no nickname true Try it Make nickname a string and run the sample again. Then write a line that prints your name in capitals, followed by its length.

markdown:
> **Experimental**
>
> WASI packaging and host compatibility are still evolving. Start with a small workload on your intended host.

WASI runs WebAssembly outside a browser. Use `--target wasi` for a command-line workload, `--target wasi-http` for an HTTP component, and [`--target js`](/building-and-deploying/javascript-and-wasm/index.html) for browsers.

## Build and run

```sh
matchbox --target wasi hello.bxs
wasmtime hello.wasm
```

The module contains a runner and your bytecode. It needs a compatible WASI Preview 1 host, such as Wasmtime.

The host controls access to files and other resources. For example, `wasmtime --dir=. hello.wasm` grants access to the current directory.

## Native Fusion

Native Fusion supports WASI alongside native, browser and ESP32 targets. Put Rust code in a `native/` directory next to the entry script, and use dependencies that support `wasm32-wasip1`.

Fusion builds require Rust, the target toolchain and the MatchBox source checkout. See [Native Fusion](/building-and-deploying/native-fusion/index.html) for setup.

## HTTP components

Package a webroot instead of a script:

```sh
matchbox --target wasi-http --webroot www --output site.wasm
```

The component needs a host implementing `wasi:http/incoming-handler`. Its build currently requires Rust, the `wasm32-wasip2` target and the MatchBox source checkout. See [WASI HTTP](/building-and-deploying/wasi-http/index.html) for setup.

## Choosing a host

WASI does not provide browser DOM APIs, JNI or JIT. File and network access depend on the host's capabilities.

OCI deployment needs a WASI-capable container runtime; an ordinary Docker installation is not enough. Start with the [WASI example](/examples/wasm_container/README/index.html).

markdown:
> **Experimental**
>
> WASI HTTP packaging and host compatibility are still evolving. Test the component on your intended host before deployment.

`--target wasi-http` turns a webroot directory into one `.wasm` component that exports the WASI HTTP incoming handler. The component serves the same files and templates as [`matchbox --serve`](/building-and-deploying/web-server/index.html), with the webroot embedded in the binary.

This is different from [`--target wasi`](/building-and-deploying/wasm-container/index.html), which packages a single script that runs once and exits.

## Build

```sh
matchbox --target wasi-http --webroot ./site --output site.wasm
```

| Flag              | Default          | Meaning               |
|:------------------|:-----------------|:----------------------|
| `--webroot <dir>` | `.`              | Directory to package. |
| `--output <file>` | `<webroot>.wasm` | Output file.          |

`--webroot` and `--output` are the only flags this target reads. Nothing is listening after the build; the component is run by a host that supports WASI HTTP.

The build:

1. Reads `boxlang.json` from the webroot for `rewrites` and `rewriteFileName`. A `websocket` block is ignored and the build prints a warning.
2. Compiles every `.bxm` and `.bxs` file in the webroot. A syntax error stops the build.
3. Embeds every file under the webroot, including `boxlang.json`, together with the compiled templates.
4. Patches that payload into a prebuilt `matchbox_wasi_http_runner` component and writes the result.

## Limits

| Limit       | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|:------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Size        | The payload must fit in a 4 MiB region of the runner (4 MiB minus 12 bytes). A larger webroot fails with "exceeds the embed capacity". Every file in the directory counts, so keep build output, `node_modules` and similar out of the webroot. |
| Native code | The build fails if the webroot has a `native` directory, a `boxlang_modules/*/native` directory, or a `.bx`, `.bxm` or `.bxs` file that contains the text `java:` or `rust:`.                                                                   |
| WebSockets  | Not supported.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Sessions    | Kept in memory of the running instance. They are not shared between instances and are lost when the instance stops.                                                                                                                             |

## Behavior

The component runs the same engine as the webroot server, so these rules apply unchanged:

* `GET`, `HEAD` and `POST` are handled; other methods return `405`.
* `.bxm` and `.bxs` files are rendered as templates, and a directory is answered by its `index.bxm` or `index.bxs`.
* Path segments that start with `.` return `403`.
* The `url`, `form`, `cookie`, `session` and `cgi` scopes are populated as described in [Web server](/building-and-deploying/web-server/index.html#scopes-in-templates).

Differences from `--serve`:

* Requests are read from the WASI HTTP request, so a POST body with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is available in `form`.
* A failure in the engine returns `500` with the error text as `text/plain`.
* `HEAD` responses carry no body.

## Requirements

The CLI builds the runner component when it is not already present. It looks for `target/wasm32-wasip2/release/matchbox_wasi_http_runner.wasm` inside the MatchBox source tree it was compiled from, and otherwise runs

```sh
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2 -p matchbox_wasi_http_runner
```

in that tree. The build therefore needs the source checkout, a Rust toolchain and the target (`rustup target add wasm32-wasip2`). A CLI downloaded as a release binary cannot find that tree unless the checkout exists at the path it was built from.

The component's exported interface is `wasi:http/incoming-handler` (the `proxy` world of the `wasi` crate). Use a host that implements it to run the file.
